name: Bacformer
description: Bacformer models a whole bacterial genome as a sequence of proteins ordered by their genomic coordinates and turns per-protein embeddings from a protein language model into contextual protein embeddings that condition each protein on the other proteins in the genome.

attributes.access: Public checkpoints on Hugging Face under macwiatrak, installed through the bacformer package; inference needs protein embeddings from a base protein language model.
attributes.identity_scope: The base size of the family, which embeds proteins with ESM-2 t12 35M and runs a 12-layer transformer of hidden size 480 over them.

sections.body: AlphaGenome progressively downsamples DNA with convolutional blocks, then uses a transformer tower and pairwise interaction blocks to represent long-range context. sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Boltz-2 first encodes the molecular inputs, alignments and optional templates into token and pair features. A Pairformer trunk updates those features and conditions atom-coordinate diffusion to generate a complex. Separate confidence and affinity modules assess the prediction; affinity classification and regression outputs answer different questions.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Boltz-1 and Boltz-2 are distinct released generations; the catalogue does not select an evaluated checkpoint. The Boltz-2 report describes training crops up to 768 tokens. This is a training-crop size rather than a universal inference maximum; affinity additionally uses a pocket crop.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Chai-1 predicts the structures of biomolecular complexes containing proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules. An AlphaFold3-like structure architecture dominated by pair-biased self-attention, with additional protein-language-model embeddings and optional inter-chain constraint features. The documented inputs are FASTA sequences, ligand SMILES and optional alignments, templates, contacts or covalent-bond restraints. The output consists of sampled complex structures; the default command produces five predictions.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNABERT-2 merges recurring DNA substrings into byte-pair tokens, then processes those tokens with a masked-language-model transformer. ALiBi supplies distance-dependent attention biases, while FlashAttention changes how attention is computed. The resulting contextual embeddings need an explicit pooling rule and prediction head for a downstream task.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESMFold predicts protein structures directly from amino-acid sequence using ESM-2 representations. ESM-2 sequence representations feed a folding trunk and structure module. The checked v1 configuration has 48 trunk blocks, eight structure-module blocks and up to four recycles. The documented inputs are protein amino-acid sequence; the ESMFold interface also accepts chains separated by a colon. The output consists of predicted PDB structure and confidence values.

name: GEARS
description: GEARS predicts transcriptional responses to single- and multi-gene perturbations from single-cell perturbation screens.

attributes.access: Public code; task-specific training data required.

profile.summary: GEARS predicts transcriptional responses to single- and multi-gene perturbations from single-cell perturbation screens.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GEARS predicts transcriptional responses to single- and multi-gene perturbations from single-cell perturbation screens. Two graph encoders represent gene coexpression and Gene Ontology perturbation similarity. Perturbation embeddings are composed with gene embeddings, then a cross-gene network and gene-specific decoders predict expression changes. The documented inputs are single-cell expression data, perturbation labels and the graph resources used by the configured model. The output consists of predicted gene-expression responses and genetic-interaction analyses.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: mRNA-FM encodes coding RNA with codon-level tokens to produce representations for downstream analysis. 12-layer transformer encoder with hidden width 1,280 and codon-level input tokens. The documented inputs are coding RNA in the correct reading frame, with sequence length divisible by three. The output consists of contextual token embeddings for a specified downstream RNA task.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Nucleotide Transformer v2 represents DNA using an encoder pretrained on multiple species. Encoder-only transformer with 6-mer tokenization, rotary position embeddings and SwiGLU feed-forward layers. The documented inputs are DNA sequences with tokenization determined by 6-mers and individual ambiguous/remainder bases. The output consists of contextual DNA embeddings and masked-token probabilities; downstream tasks need adaptation.

profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Deep neural network architecture and Generating training and test sets; README.md: Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Pangolin predicts splice-site strength and changes caused by genetic variants. Dilated convolutional network with 16 residual blocks and skip connections; separate probability and usage outputs for heart, liver, brain and testis. The documented inputs are VCF or CSV variants, reference FASTA and matching gene annotations; custom sequence inference is also available. The output consists of predicted increases/decreases in splice-site strength and their positions.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Deep neural network architecture and Generating training and test sets; README.md: Usage

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Pangolin implementation; gene-annotation database and selected weights must be recorded with a run. 5,000 bases upstream and downstream each output position; minimum 10,001-base input for one prediction, with 15,000-base training blocks producing 5,000 central outputs.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProkBERT is a family of microbial DNA encoders used for sequence representation, promoter prediction and phage identification. MegatronBERT-based encoder using local-context-aware k-mer tokenization, learned relative key/value positions and masked-language pretraining. The documented inputs are microbial DNA segments tokenized with the selected variant. The output consists of sequence representations or predictions from separately fine-tuned promoter/phage heads.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: ProkBERT-mini (6-mer, shift 1), mini-c (single base), mini-long (6-mer, shift 2), plus promoter/phage fine-tunes. The paper reports maximum sequence lengths of 1,024bp for mini and 2,048bp for mini-long; tokenization stride distinguishes the variants.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProteinMPNN converts a supplied backbone into a graph whose edges encode interatomic distances. Message-passing layers update node and edge features, and an autoregressive decoder samples amino acids while conditioning on the backbone and previously assigned residues. Fixed residues, tied positions and chain choices change the design task and must accompany its result.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RhoFold+ predicts RNA three-dimensional structures from RNA sequence with alignment information. RNA-FM embeddings and MSA representations enter the Rhoformer transformer stack; a geometry-aware invariant-point-attention structure module predicts frames and torsion angles with recycling. The documented inputs are RNA FASTA (A, U, G, C), optionally a supplied MSA; an MSA is otherwise generated by the full workflow. The output consists of three-dimensional PDB models, predicted distograms, secondary structure and per-residue confidence.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RNA-FM converts an RNA sequence into one token per nucleotide. Twelve transformer encoder blocks use self-attention to produce a 640-dimensional representation at each position. During pretraining, the model learns to recover masked nucleotides from their surrounding sequence. The resulting representations can be supplied to a separately specified downstream model; they are not, by themselves, a structure or functional prediction.

sections.body: The nucleotide-based rna_fm_t12 and codon-based mrna_fm_t12 interfaces are distinct. The original RNA-FM paper sets a training input-length limit of 1,024 and describes a usable limit of 1,022 nucleotides. That limit should not be assigned to mRNA-FM without checking its separate configuration.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: scFoundation embeds gene identity and continuous expression together with source and target read-depth indicators. Its encoder processes only nonzero, unmasked genes. Those contextual embeddings are combined with zero and mask embeddings before a Performer decoder predicts expression across the full gene vocabulary. Pooled encoder outputs represent cells; decoder outputs provide gene-level context.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SpliceAI reads one-hot-encoded DNA through dilated convolutional residual blocks. Skip connections combine features at different depths, and a softmax layer assigns acceptor, donor or neither probabilities to the central positions. The 10kb version requires 5kb of sequence on each side of a scored position; variant scoring compares the reference and alternate predictions.
sections.source_locator: Jaganathan et al., Cell 2019, STAR Methods: SpliceAI architecture and Model training and testing (pp. e2–e3); README.md: usage and License

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper studies 80nt, 400nt, 2kb and 10kb receptive spans. Variant scoring averages five independently trained models; these are not five different assay results. SpliceAI-10k uses 5,000 flanking bases on each side. An input of length l + 10,000 produces predictions for l central positions; receptive span is distinct from maximum input length.
sections.source_locator: Jaganathan et al., Cell 2019, STAR Methods: SpliceAI architecture and Model training and testing (pp. e2–e3); README.md: usage and License

profile.summary: AlphaFold 3 predicts three-dimensional structures of complexes containing proteins, nucleic acids and other molecular components. It combines a Pairformer representation network with an atomic-coordinate diffusion model. This entry describes the model and local implementation; the hosted AlphaFold Server has a separate profile.
profile.summary_source_locator: Abstract; Model architecture; README: Installation and Usage

sections.title: Joint structure prediction
sections.body: Sequence, chemical and evolutionary features feed a Pairformer, which builds representations of individual tokens and their relationships. A diffusion module then predicts atomic coordinates. Separate heads estimate confidence. The paper describes 48 Pairformer blocks; the architecture models complexes jointly rather than treating every partner as a separately folded structure.
sections.source_locator: Main text: Model architecture; Fig. 1d and Fig. 2

sections.title: Training and evaluation context
sections.body: The standard model uses a structural training cutoff of 30 September 2021. The dedicated PoseBusters Methods section reports a separate model with a 30 September 2019 cutoff, although other training passages disagree (see limitations). Model seeds, templates, input information and ranking also affect the reported comparison; paper evaluation variants are not automatically identical to current downloadable weights.
sections.source_locator: Main paper Methods: Training regime, Inference regime and PoseBusters; supplement Section 5.2

sections.title: Local access
sections.body: The pinned repository provides inference code and a direct Google-hosted weights download. Its README is more current on access than the server FAQ, which still describes an application form. Code and model parameters have different licences; the server output terms should not be substituted for the local weights terms.
sections.source_locator: README: Obtaining Model Parameters and Licences; LICENSE; weights terms: Key things to know; FAQ: model access

sections.title: Training data and provenance
sections.body: Training combines experimental PDB structures with approximately 41 million predicted protein monomers, about 25,000 disorder-focused protein complexes and about 65,000 predicted RNA structures. The supplement also lists transcription-factor examples used during fine-tuning. Its sequence-search resources include UniRef90, UniProt, BFD/Uniclust30, MGnify, Rfam and RNAcentral. These resources have different versions and dates: the structural training cutoff is not a cutoff for every sequence database.

profile.summary: Boltz predicts biomolecular complex structures; Boltz-2 also predicts binding affinity.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Boltz-2 first encodes the molecular inputs, alignments and optional templates into token and pair features. A Pairformer trunk updates those features and conditions atom-coordinate diffusion to generate a complex. Separate confidence and affinity modules assess the prediction; affinity classification and regression outputs answer different questions. This describes the Boltz-2 generation; a Boltz-1 result must retain its original checkpoint and prediction procedure.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNABERT-2 merges recurring DNA substrings into byte-pair tokens, then processes those tokens with a masked-language-model transformer. ALiBi supplies distance-dependent attention biases, while FlashAttention changes how attention is computed. The resulting contextual embeddings need an explicit pooling rule and prediction head for a downstream task.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESMFold predicts protein structures directly from amino-acid sequence using ESM-2 representations. ESM-2 sequence representations feed a folding trunk and structure module. sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GEARS predicts transcriptional responses to single- and multi-gene perturbations from single-cell perturbation screens. Two graph encoders represent gene coexpression and Gene Ontology perturbation similarity. Perturbation embeddings are composed with gene embeddings, then a cross-gene network and gene-specific decoders predict expression changes. The documented inputs are single-cell expression data, perturbation labels and the graph resources used by the configured model. The output consists of predicted gene-expression responses and genetic-interaction analyses.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MSAlign retrieves candidate molecules from tandem mass spectra by aligning pretrained molecular and spectral representations. sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Nucleotide Transformer is a family of DNA encoders pretrained on human or multispecies sequence corpora. Encoder-only transformers with 6-mer tokens; v1 uses learned positional encodings and v2 uses rotary positions and SwiGLU. The documented inputs are DNA sequences tokenized into 6-mers, with single-base handling of N and remainder bases. The output consists of contextual representations used in specified downstream prediction workflows.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProteinMPNN converts a supplied backbone into a graph whose edges encode interatomic distances. Message-passing layers update node and edge features, and an autoregressive decoder samples amino acids while conditioning on the backbone and previously assigned residues. Fixed residues, tied positions and chain choices change the design task and must accompany its result.

profile.summary: RNA-FM learns contextual representations of RNA nucleotides for downstream RNA analyses.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Quick Start, embedding examples and RNA foundation model comparison table

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RNA-FM converts an RNA sequence into one token per nucleotide. Twelve transformer encoder blocks use self-attention to produce a 640-dimensional representation at each position. During pretraining, the model learns to recover masked nucleotides from their surrounding sequence. The resulting representations can be supplied to a separately specified downstream model; they are not, by themselves, a structure or functional prediction.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The nucleotide-based rna_fm_t12 and codon-based mrna_fm_t12 interfaces are distinct. The original RNA-FM paper sets a training input-length limit of 1,024 and describes a usable limit of 1,022 nucleotides. That limit should not be assigned to mRNA-FM without checking its separate configuration.

profile.summary: SpliceAI annotates sequence variants with predicted splice acceptor and donor changes.
profile.summary_source_locator: Jaganathan et al., Cell 2019, STAR Methods: SpliceAI architecture and Model training and testing (pp. e2–e3); README.md: usage and License

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SpliceAI reads one-hot-encoded DNA through dilated convolutional residual blocks. Skip connections combine features at different depths, and a softmax layer assigns acceptor, donor or neither probabilities to the central positions. The 10kb version requires 5kb of sequence on each side of a scored position; variant scoring compares the reference and alternate predictions.
sections.source_locator: Jaganathan et al., Cell 2019, STAR Methods: SpliceAI architecture and Model training and testing (pp. e2–e3); README.md: usage and License

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper studies 80nt, 400nt, 2kb and 10kb receptive spans. Variant scoring averages five independently trained models; these are not five different assay results. SpliceAI-10k uses 5,000 flanking bases on each side. An input of length l + 10,000 produces predictions for l central positions; receptive span is distinct from maximum input length.
sections.source_locator: Jaganathan et al., Cell 2019, STAR Methods: SpliceAI architecture and Model training and testing (pp. e2–e3); README.md: usage and License

sections.body: The TAPE Bepler comparison uses a protein representation that combines bidirectional language modelling with supervised structural pretraining. name: CodonBERT
description: BERT-style language model of mRNA coding sequences at codon resolution.

attributes.source_locator: Reference 124 in the SI (Li et al.); SI A.3.11 ('BERT-style model focused on codon usage')

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: CodonBERT is a language model for the coding regions of mRNA, built by Sanofi for mRNA vaccine and therapeutic design. It reads a coding sequence codon by codon and outputs an embedding for each codon. These embeddings can be fine-tuned to predict properties such as protein expression and mRNA degradation, to help choose among the many mRNA sequences that encode the same protein.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results (first paragraph)

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: CodonBERT is a BERT model of 12 bidirectional transformer encoder layers, each with 12 attention heads and hidden size 768. Each codon is one token: five symbols (A, U, G, C, N) in three positions give 125 codons, plus five special tokens, for a vocabulary of 130. The input is a pair of sequences joined by a separator, embedded with codon, position and segment embeddings. Pretraining combined two tasks: masked language modelling over codons, and sequence taxonomy prediction, in which the model predicts whether the two sequences come from the same one of 14 taxonomic categories. For downstream tasks, the embeddings feed additional trainable layers.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Model architecture'; Results

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pretrained PyTorch model is released, as a single zip file (CodonBERT.zip, 954,923,856 bytes, last modified 8 May 2024) on a Sanofi download server rather than a versioned model hub, so the file has no revision identifier beyond its date. The repository holds pretraining and fine-tuning scripts, the NCBI IDs of all 10 million pretraining sequences, a held-out evaluation set, and the downstream datasets including an internal Sanofi set (MLOS.csv). A result should name the repository commit (451a1b16 read here) and the zip file's date or checksum.
sections.source_locator: README: CodonBERT, Dataset; HTTP headers of CodonBERT.zip

facts.value: A contextual embedding for each codon; extract_embed.py saves the last hidden layer per sequence, without the start and end special tokens, to a pickle file. Fine-tuned heads output task predictions such as protein expression or mRNA degradation.

profile.summary: DeCodon is a generative language model for protein-coding DNA that works one codon at a time. Given an NCBI Taxonomy ID for an organism, it writes new coding sequences for that organism. It is the decoder half of the cdsFM suite, released with the encoder model EnCodon, and was pretrained on coding sequences from the NCBI Genomes database.

sections.body: Each token is one of the 64 codons or a special token. DeCodon is loaded as a causal language model: its configuration marks it as a decoder with 12 hidden layers, 16 attention heads, hidden size 1024 and rotary position embeddings. To generate, the wrapper builds a prompt from the organism's taxonomy ID in angle brackets, so the model writes a sequence conditioned on the organism, and stops at the separator token. The same wrapper also offers embedding extraction and variant scoring.

profile.summary: EnCodon is a language model for protein-coding DNA that reads a coding sequence one codon at a time and returns a numerical embedding of it. The embeddings can be used as features or fine-tuned, and the package also scores codon variants by comparing model probabilities. It is part of the cdsFM suite, released with the generative model DeCodon, and was pretrained on coding sequences from the NCBI Genomes database.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: introduction; Sequence Embedding Extraction with EnCodon; bioRxiv abstract; cdsfm/encodon/_auto.py: score_variants

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each token is one of the 64 codons or one of 5 special tokens, and a start token and an end token are added around each sequence. EnCodon is loaded as a masked language model with rotary position embeddings. To embed a sequence, the wrapper runs the model, takes the hidden states of a chosen layer and averages them over the codon positions, leaving out the two special tokens. To score a variant, it compares the log probability of the alternative codon with that of the reference codon, either in the wild-type sequence or with the position masked.
sections.source_locator: README: Tokenization; config.json; cdsfm/encodon/_auto.py: get_embeddings, score_variants

sections.body: Four EnCodon checkpoints are listed, in two sizes. encodon-80M and encodon-620M are the pretrained checkpoints; encodon-80M-euk and encodon-620M-euk are described only as eukaryotic experts. The encodon-80M checkpoint has 6 layers, 8 attention heads and hidden size 1024; the encodon-620M checkpoint has 12 layers, 16 heads and hidden size 2048. The configs of the euk checkpoints were not read. This page read encodon-80M at revision 81702e23, encodon-80M-euk at 746f9f3a, encodon-620M at 87958432 and encodon-620M-euk at 3597b284. attributes.access: Published checkpoint songlab/gpn-msa-sapiens on Hugging Face; inference with the gpn package ('gpn msa {vep,logits,embedding}'). The repository marks GPN-MSA as deprecated in favour of GPN-Star and no longer maintains training.

profile.summary: GPN-MSA is a DNA language model that scores human single-nucleotide variants genome-wide. It reads a window of the human genome together with the aligned sequence of other vertebrates, and scores a variant by how much less likely the alternate allele is than the reference. Its developers now mark it as deprecated in favour of GPN-Star.
profile.summary_source_locator: docs/models/gpn-msa.md, opening paragraph; model card title; cli.md, GPN section on the output score

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The published checkpoint is a 12-layer Transformer encoder (hidden size 768, 12 attention heads) trained as a masked language model. Each position is given the human nucleotide and the aligned nucleotides of the other species in the whole-genome alignment as auxiliary features, so the model predicts a masked human base from its sequence context and from what other vertebrates carry at the same site. A variant's score is the alternate-minus-reference log-likelihood ratio at its position, averaged over the forward and reverse-complement orientations. Negative values mean the alternate allele is less likely than the reference under the model.
sections.source_locator: config.json: architectures, num_hidden_layers, hidden_size, num_attention_heads, n_aux_features; cli.md: GPN and GPN-MSA sections on the output score; model card title

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One human checkpoint is published, songlab/gpn-msa-sapiens, trained on humans and 89 other vertebrates. The repository supports inference from it and no longer maintains GPN-MSA training or dataset construction. Inference needs a local alignment store whose target assembly, species count, species order and preprocessing match the checkpoint. Genome-wide hg38 scores are published as a dataset, so most uses do not need to run the model. A result should say whether it used the published scores or ran inference, and with which window size.

profile.summary: RNABERT is a small RNA language model from Keio University that turns each base of a non-coding RNA sequence into a numerical vector (an embedding) that reflects its sequence context and secondary structure. It reads RNA sequences in FASTA format and outputs per-base embeddings, which the authors use to align RNAs by structure and to cluster them into RNA families.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Introduction; README.md: Data processing, Earn embeddings

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each base gets a 120-dimensional token embedding plus a position embedding, and the sum passes through six Transformer layers. The output is a context-sensitive embedding for every base. Training alternates two tasks. In masked language modelling (MLM), some bases are hidden and predicted from the rest. In structural alignment learning (SAL), pairs of sequences from Rfam seed alignments are aligned using their embeddings, so that bases aligned in the reference alignment get similar embeddings. A structural alignment of two RNAs is then computed from the embeddings with the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Figure 2 caption; Introduction; Discussion

The README says this model was trained on the full Rfam 14.3 dataset (about 400 nucleotides), while the paper describes MLM pre-training on 76 237 human small ncRNAs from RNAcentral and SAL training on Rfam alignments (TrainSet-A or TrainSet-B). Which of the paper's settings the download matches is not stated. A result should cite the repository commit and say that the Google Drive model was used.

profile.summary: RNAErnie is an RNA language model that turns an RNA sequence into embeddings for downstream prediction. During pretraining it uses known RNA motifs as prior knowledge and masks them at random, alongside the usual masked language modelling. Its developers fine-tune it for RNA sequence classification, RNA-RNA interaction prediction and RNA secondary structure prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The original RNAErnie is built on the ERNIE model in PaddlePaddle and pretrained with masked language modelling on RNAcentral sequences of up to 512 nucleotides. The released checkpoint combines the BERT, ERNIE and motif masking strategies. Downstream, the developers offer an optional two-stage, type-guided fine-tuning. For RNA secondary structure prediction the repository uses a folding module compiled from mxfold2. The authors' later PyTorch checkpoint is a BERT masked language model with 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads and an 11-token vocabulary.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Pre-training, Extract RNA Sequence Embeddings, Downstream Tasks; config.json of the PyTorch checkpoint

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are two lines of checkpoints. The original PaddlePaddle model from the paper, with masking-strategy variants and task-specific fine-tuned weights, is distributed through Google Drive folders linked from the README; an ad-hoc variant pretrained with an extra classification loss and a 1-epoch checkpoint are also linked. In June 2024 the developers trained a separate PyTorch model from scratch with a maximum length of 2048 on a newer RNAcentral release of about 31 million sequences, and published it on Hugging Face (now LLM-EDA/RNAErnie); its tokenisation differs slightly from the original. A result should say which of these checkpoints was used.

run_guide.summary: Set up the original PaddlePaddle RNAErnie environment and extract embeddings for three example RNA sequences with the pretrained checkpoint.
prerequisites: Conda, and a GPU: the environment installs paddlepaddle-gpu 2.3.2 and the example sets the device to gpu.

The pretrained checkpoint files (.pdparams and .json) downloaded by hand from the Google Drive folder linked in the README and placed in ./output/BERT,ERNIE,MOTIF,PROMPT so that output/BERT,ERNIE,MOTIF,PROMPT/checkpoint_final/ exists. The README does not state the folder layout inside the download.
The environment file pins Linux conda builds and a Tsinghua mirror channel, so it may not resolve on other platforms.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/CatIIIIIIII/RNAErnie.git
cd ./RNAErnie
git checkout --detach b5e4c1cfdc6f53101111823abaddcab00c43b0d3
steps.explanation: Clones the repository as in the README. The checkout line is added to pin the commit read for this page.

conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate RNAErnie
steps.explanation: Creates the conda environment named RNAErnie with Python 3.8 and PaddlePaddle.

steps.title: Extract embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import paddle
from rna_ernie import BatchConverter
from paddlenlp.transformers import ErnieModel

# ========== Set device
paddle.set_device("gpu")

# ========== Prepare Data
data = [
    ("RNA1", "GGGUGCGAUCAUACCAGCACUAAUGCCCUCCUGGGAAGUCCUCGUGUUGCACCCCU"),
    ("RNA2", "GGGUGUCGCUCAGUUGGUAGAGUGCUUGCCUGGCAUGCAAGAAACCUUGGUUCAAUCCCCAGCACUGCA"),
    ("RNA3", "CGAUUCNCGUUCCC--CCGCCUCCA"),
]

# ========== Batch Converter
batch_converter = BatchConverter(k_mer=1,
                                  vocab_path="./data/vocab/vocab_1MER.txt",
                                  batch_size=256,
                                  max_seq_len=512)

# ========== RNAErnie Model
rna_ernie = ErnieModel.from_pretrained("output/BERT,ERNIE,MOTIF,PROMPT/checkpoint_final/")
rna_ernie.eval()

# call batch_converter to convert sequences to batch inputs
for names, _, inputs_ids in batch_converter(data):
    with paddle.no_grad():
        # extract whole sequence embeddings
        embeddings = rna_ernie(inputs_ids)[0].detach()
        # extract [CLS] token embedding
        embeddings_cls = embeddings[:, 0, :]
        print(names, embeddings.shape, embeddings_cls.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's embedding example, run from the repository root and wrapped in a heredoc; the commented-out FASTA line was dropped and a print of the names and tensor shapes was added.

outputs: Whole-sequence token embeddings and [CLS] embeddings for each batch of input sequences, held as Paddle tensors.

profile.summary: UTR-LM is a language model for the 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) of mRNA, the stretch before the coding sequence that strongly affects how well an mRNA is translated. It reads a 5' UTR sequence and, after fine-tuning, predicts mean ribosome loading, translation efficiency or mRNA expression level. Pretraining combines masked language modelling with labels computed from the sequence, such as secondary structure and minimum free energy.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: UTR-LM is built on a modified copy of the ESM-2 transformer code, shipped in the repository. The reported settings are 6 transformer layers, 16 attention heads and an embedding size of 128. Pretraining uses masked language modelling (MLM) and, in the recommended variants, also predicts the minimum free energy (MFE) and/or the secondary structure of the sequence. For downstream tasks the developers fine-tune the whole model and feed the [CLS]-token embedding to a predictor trained with Huber loss.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Install step 3; General Parameters; UTR-LM pretraining process

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository holds 16 pretrained checkpoint files under Model/Pretrained, named by their pretraining variant (ESM2, ESM2SI, ESM2SS, ESM2SISS, ESM2DSD) and data split, plus 182 files under Model/Downstream for the MRL, TE and EL tasks. The README's own example pretraining command passes --heads 6 --embed_dim 16, which disagrees with the 16 heads and embedding size 128 listed under General Parameters and in the checkpoint file names. A result should name the exact checkpoint file and the repository commit. A runnable copy is also published as a CodeOcean capsule.

limitations.text: The code is GPL-3.0, which carries copyleft obligations for derived work.
Installation needs a modified copy of the ESM source code to be moved by hand into the environment's site-packages, so the package will not work from a plain pip install.
The example commands are written for a specific machine: the training and task data come from Google Drive links, and the README notes paths must be changed to your own.
The examples launch torch.distributed with up to four GPUs, and the requirements file pins a full conda environment with local build paths, which will not resolve elsewhere.

run_guide.summary: Set up the UTR-LM environment with its modified ESM code, then fine-tune a pretrained checkpoint for translation efficiency on the Muscle cell line.
prerequisites: Conda, and a CUDA GPU: the commands launch torch.distributed and set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.
Task data downloaded by hand from the Google Drive folder linked in the README (for the TE and EL task, the Muscle, pc3 or HEK cell-line data).
Paths in the commands changed to your own directories, as the README states.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/a96123155/UTR-LM.git
cd UTR-LM
git checkout --detach b77b589bf182eb9de6a1a5024fa09d44294d94fc
steps.explanation: The README does not give a clone command; this clones the repository named in the README and pins the commit read for this page. Later commands are run from the repository root.
steps.source_locator: README.md: Install step 2 and Instruction Example

steps.title: Create the environment
steps.shell:
conda create -n UTRLM python==3.9.13
conda activate UTRLM
pip install -r utrlm_requirements.txt
steps.explanation: The README's environment steps. The requirements file pins a full conda environment including local build paths, so the plain pip list in the README may be needed instead.

steps.title: Install the modified ESM code
steps.shell:
pip install fair-esm
find -name esm
scp -r ./Scripts/esm ./.conda/envs/UTRLM/lib/python3.9/site-packages/
steps.explanation: Installs fair-esm, then copies the repository's modified esm folder over it. The destination path must match your own environment.

steps.title: Fine-tune for translation efficiency
steps.shell:
cd ./Scripts/UTRLM_downstream
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python3 -m torch.distributed.launch --nproc_per_node=1 --master_port 9001 MJ4_Finetune_extract_append_predictor_CellLine_10fold-lr-huber-DDP.py --device_ids 0 --cell_line Muscle --label_type te_log --seq_type utr --inp_len 100 --huber_loss --modelfile ./Model/ESM2SI_3.1_fiveSpeciesCao_6layers_16heads_128embedsize_4096batchToks_MLMLossMin.pkl --finetune --bos_emb --lr 1e-2 --dropout3 0.2 --epochs 300 --prefix TE_ESM2SI_3.1.1e-2.M.dropout2
steps.explanation: The README's TE and EL command for the Muscle cell line, using the ESM2SI_3.1 pretrained checkpoint. Change --cell_line to pc3 or HEK, and --label_type to rnaseq_log for the expression-level task.
steps.source_locator: README.md: 2. For TE and EL task

outputs: Fine-tuning logs and a trained predictor checkpoint for the chosen cell line and label type. The README does not state the output paths; the prediction notebook MJ5_Predict_and_Extract_Attention_Embedding.ipynb reads such a checkpoint to produce predictions, embeddings and attention.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The checkpoint path in the README's TE command is ./Model/ESM2SI_3.1_... while the repository stores that file under Model/Pretrained/, so the path needs adjusting.
Data must be fetched by hand from Google Drive, with no checksum.

name: DeepAffinity
description: Semi-supervised deep learning model that predicts compound-protein affinity from a compound SMILES string and a structure-annotated protein sequence, using recurrent encoders followed by convolutional layers.

entity_classification.rationale: The cited paper names DeepAffinity as a learned compound-protein affinity predictor. This record covers the method family described there; no checkpoint or variant is implied.
entity_classification.source_locator: arXiv:1806.07537v2 title and abstract, p.1; §§2.4-2.5, p.4

profile.summary: DeepAffinity predicts compound-protein affinity from a compound SMILES string and a structure property-annotated protein sequence (SPS), using pretrained recurrent seq2seq encoders followed by convolutional layers.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GRU seq2seq auto-encoders are first trained without labels on compound SMILES and protein SPS strings. In the unified RNN-CNN model, a 1D convolution and max-pooling layer is added after each encoder, the two outputs are concatenated and passed through two fully connected layers, and the whole pipeline is trained end to end with the pretrained encoders as initialisation. A separate RNN-CNN baseline keeps the encoders fixed.

sections.title: Protein representation
sections.body: In the original paper, SPS strings group residues into secondary structure elements using secondary structure and solvent accessibility predicted from sequence by SSpro/ACCpro.

sections.title: Variants
sections.body: The paper also describes separate, marginalized and joint attention mechanisms trained jointly with the encoders and CNN, and a unified RNN/GCNN-CNN variant that replaces the compound RNN with a graph CNN.
sections.source_locator: arXiv:1806.07537v2 §2.5, p.4 and PDF p.8; README Table of contents

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SMILES strings and protein sequences are label-encoded characters. Each passes through its own block of three 1D convolutional layers, where the second and third layers have two and three times the filters of the first, followed by max-pooling. The two pooled vectors are concatenated and fed into fully connected layers of 1,024, 1,024 and 512 units, with dropout after the first two, and a regression output trained with mean squared error.
sections.source_locator: arXiv:1801.10193v2 input representation, PDF p.4; Proposed model and Figure 2, PDF pp.7-8

sections.title: Original evaluation
sections.body: The paper evaluates on the Davis kinase dataset (Kd) and the KIBA dataset. It fixes maximum lengths of 85 SMILES and 1,200 protein characters for Davis and 100 and 1,000 for KIBA.

profile.summary: LIMBER is an RNA language model for non-coding RNA. It reads an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and returns per-nucleotide embeddings and masked-token predictions, which the authors use for secondary-structure prediction, RNA family classification and mutational fitness scoring.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md at commit 72a328a: Overview and Quick start; preprint abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LIMBER stacks two kinds of layer in a repeating Transformer, Transformer, Mamba pattern. The Transformer layers use bidirectional self-attention, which relates any two positions directly; the authors link this to the long-range coupling that base pairing leaves in a sequence. The Mamba layers are selective state-space layers that process the sequence in order. The model is pretrained by masked language modelling: 15% of nucleotide positions are selected, and of those 80% are replaced by a mask token, 10% by a random nucleotide and 10% left unchanged. Tokenisation is one token per nucleotide over a 10-token vocabulary; T is mapped to U and any other symbol to N.
sections.source_locator: README.md at commit 72a328a: Overview; Model zoo; Tokenization; Pretraining

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Five LIMBER sizes are released, from 10.2M to 664.3M parameters, with size-matched pure-Transformer and pure-Mamba models trained on the same data. The README counts 25 checkpoints in one Hugging Face repository, one subfolder per model, including data-fraction, training-epoch and shape ablations. A result should name the subfolder it used: LIMBER-macro, LIMBER-meso and LIMBER-nano differ in depth and width, not only in size. The Hugging Face repository was at revision d2d6ae6 when read on 2026-11-26.
sections.source_locator: README.md at commit 72a328a: Model zoo; Hugging Face file listing at revision d2d6ae6

sections.title: What the authors report
sections.body: The authors fine-tuned LIMBER and each baseline themselves under one protocol. They report a median flexible F1 of 0.895 on bpRNA TS0 and 0.816 on Rivas TestSetB for LIMBER-macro, and 99.2% accuracy on the 13-class nRC benchmark. On IRES identification and 5'UTR mean ribosome load, RiNALMo-giga scores higher than LIMBER-macro on most metrics in the same tables. These are author-reported figures and are not yet recorded as results in this database.
sections.source_locator: README.md at commit 72a328a: Results tables for secondary structure, nRC, IRES and mean ribosome load

run_guide.summary: Install the dependencies, download LIMBER-macro from Hugging Face and run one forward pass to get embeddings for an RNA sequence.
prerequisites: Python 3.10 or later with PyTorch 2.x.

An NVIDIA GPU with CUDA: the quick start moves tensors to a CUDA device and the Mamba layers need the mamba-ssm and causal-conv1d packages. The memory needed is not stated; LIMBER-macro has 664.3M parameters.
Network access to huggingface.co for the weights. No licence is stated for the code or the weights.

steps.title: Get the code at the reviewed commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/ziyaow1010/LIMBER.git
cd LIMBER
git checkout --detach 72a328aaa52a46a8916496eddb2feff86933a1d3
steps.explanation: Checkout wrapper: the detached commit is the revision this guide was read from. The repository does not publish tagged releases.

steps.title: Install the dependencies
steps.shell:
pip install torch transformers safetensors huggingface_hub
pip install causal-conv1d mamba-ssm
steps.explanation: The second line installs the packages the Mamba layers require.

steps.title: Download LIMBER-macro and run a forward pass
steps.shell: python scripts/load_hybrid650.py --seq GGGCUAUUAGCUCAGUUGGUUAGAGCGCACCCCUGAUAAGGGUGAGGUCGCUGAUUCGAAUUCAGCAUAGCCCA
steps.explanation: The script downloads the LIMBER-macro checkpoint and runs it on the given sequence. Without --seq it uses a built-in example.

steps.title: Get embeddings from Python
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from scripts.load_hybrid650 import load_hybrid, encode, embed

model, _ = load_hybrid()
ids = torch.tensor([encode("GGGCUAUUAGCUCAGUUGG")]).cuda()
logits = model(input_ids=ids, attention_mask=torch.ones_like(ids)).logits
h = embed(model, ids)
print(logits.shape, h.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's Python example, wrapped in a heredoc so it can be pasted into a shell. Run it from the repository root.

outputs: Masked-token logits of shape [1, L+2, 10].
Per-nucleotide embeddings of shape [1, L+2, 1280]; position 0 is the pooled sequence representation.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
Other checkpoints load through HybridMambaConfig and HybridMambaForMaskedLM with the model_config.json in their subfolder; this guide covers LIMBER-macro only.
Sequences longer than 1,022 nucleotides must be cropped or split before encoding.

profile.summary: Ladon is a foundation model for bulk RNA sequencing of tumours, built by the company Blank Bio. It learns from millions of RNA-seq profiles by reconstructing masked parts of isoform-level expression, and its embeddings are then used to predict patient survival, recurrence and response to treatment. The developers present it as a way to make RNA-based predictions that still hold in clinical trials and cohorts the model was not fitted on.
profile.summary_source_locator: Report page 1 (abstract); page 2, Introducing Ladon

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Ladon is a transformer encoder-decoder of 3 billion parameters. It is pretrained self-supervised, by masked token reconstruction on isoform-level expression profiles, so it can learn from samples without outcome labels. For clinical use the developers then mid-train it with supervision to predict patient and tumour characteristics such as disease stage, age, tumour grade and genomic alterations, together with clinical outcomes. They then discard the prediction heads, freeze the encoder and fit simple outcome models, such as linear Cox survival models, on its embeddings. The report does not describe the layers, tokenisation or training corpus in more detail.
sections.source_locator: Report page 2, Introducing Ladon; page 11, Methods: Ladon representations; page 6; page 28, Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The report describes one model family and several adaptations of it (pretrained encoder, supervised mid-training with survival or response labels), and shows models of several sizes and training steps in its scaling figures, but names no released checkpoint. No weights, code or data release is listed with the report. On 2026-11-26 the GitHub organisation blankbio had 0 public repositories and the Hugging Face organisation BlankBio had 0 models and 0 datasets. Results from Ladon cannot be reproduced independently from public material.
sections.source_locator: Report pages 11, 41 to 42 (Figures 20 and 21, Methods: Reconstruction loss); GitHub org API; Hugging Face org overview

sections.title: Evaluation in the report
sections.body: Every result is reported on a setting not used for fitting: a held-out trial, another cohort or another platform. Survival models fitted on TCGA were applied unchanged to CPTAC and the reverse; the developers report Ladon ahead of differential gene expression signatures, BulkRNABERT and BulkFormer, and that adding Ladon to clinical covariates improved survival prediction in all 12 target cohorts. They also report better response prediction for immunotherapy than PD-L1 expression, recovery of isoform usage from gene-level counts (median Pearson r of 0.81 across 3,000 genes in held-out tumours), and cell-composition inference from single-cell references. All of these are the developers' own results in an unreviewed report.
sections.source_locator: Report pages 2 to 3, 5 to 6, 26 to 27

profile.summary: BioFM is a genomic foundation model from M42 Health that reads DNA together with biological context. Its BioToken tokeniser encodes genetic variants and annotated regions (such as genes and regulatory elements) directly in the input, instead of treating DNA as bases only. The model produces embeddings for variants or sequences, which are used with simple classifiers to predict effects on expression, splicing and pathogenicity; it can also generate DNA sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; model card: Model Details; README: Quick Start

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: BioFM is a decoder-only (causal) transformer on the Mistral architecture, with 23 layers and hidden size 640. Its input is DNA annotated with BioTokens: tokens that carry variant information and genomic annotations alongside the bases. For a variant, the package builds an upstream and a downstream sequence, each ending at the variant and half the evaluation context long; the downstream one is reverse complemented. Reference and mutated embeddings are each averaged over the two directions and then concatenated, giving a vector twice the embedding size. For plain sequences the embedding is taken from the last token. Downstream predictions use linear probing on these embeddings.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model Details; config.json; README: Features, Creating Variant Embeddings, Sequence Embeddings, Prediction of Variant Effect

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is released: m42-health/BioFM-265M. A result should name it and its Hugging Face revision; this page read revision 52218bbd. The biofm-eval package is version 0.1.0. The README includes a script to reproduce the paper's variant benchmark by linear probing on the m42-health/variant-benchmark dataset with chromosome-based folds. Training ran on an NVIDIA DGX cluster with H100 GPUs using PyTorch FSDP.

run_guide.summary: Install the biofm-eval package at a pinned commit and extract embeddings for two short DNA sequences with BioFM-265M.
prerequisites: conda, to create a Python 3.11 environment. The package requires Python >=3.11, torch>=2.5.1 and transformers>=4.46.1.
No GPU is required; the developers tested on a MacBook M2 Pro with 16GB memory and on Linux with an H100.
Code and weights are CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial). The weights are not gated.

steps.title: Create the environment
steps.shell:
conda create -n biofm-eval-env python=3.11
conda activate biofm-eval-env
steps.explanation: Creates and activates the Python 3.11 environment named in the README.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit and install
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/m42-health/biofm-eval.git
cd biofm-eval
git checkout --detach fcb86e1cb699bf29d220eae173e5042ba3f4ad3d
pip install -e .
steps.explanation: The README's clone and install commands. The checkout line is added to get the commit this page was written from.

steps.title: Extract sequence embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from biofm_eval import AnnotatedModel, AnnotationTokenizer, Embedder
import torch

MODEL_PATH = "m42-health/BioFM-265M"
TOKENIZER_PATH = "m42-health/BioFM-265M"

model = AnnotatedModel.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_PATH,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
tokenizer = AnnotationTokenizer.from_pretrained(TOKENIZER_PATH)

embedder = Embedder(model, tokenizer)

input_sequences = ['AGCT', 'GACTGCA']
sequence_embedding = embedder.get_sequence_embeddings(input_sequences)
print(f'Embedding dimension: {sequence_embedding.shape}')
PY
steps.explanation: The README's sequence embedding example, wrapped in a shell heredoc with its comments removed. It downloads BioFM-265M and needs no other input files.

outputs: A printed tensor shape: one embedding per input sequence, of shape (num_sequences, embedding_dim), taken from the last token.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
Variant embeddings need a GRCh38 reference FASTA, a GENCODE v38 GFF3 and a VCF, which the user must download; the README gives the download pages.
Non-commercial licence for both code and weights.

profile.summary: DeepGene is a DNA foundation model that learns from a pan-genome graph rather than a single reference sequence, so that genetic variation across individuals is part of what it sees in pretraining. It is a transformer encoder with rotary position embeddings, built to handle sequences of different lengths. The pretrained model is fine-tuned for sequence classification tasks such as promoter prediction and the Genome Understanding Evaluation (GUE) tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; README introduction and Model Fine-tuning; finetune.py

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is a RoFormer, a transformer encoder with rotary position embeddings, pretrained as a masked language model. The code's default configuration has 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads, a vocabulary of 4096 tokens and 5120 positions; pretraining builds the model from this default configuration. The pretraining data comes from a Minigraph pan-genome graph: the processing script reads the graph's sequence segments and edges and tokenises them with the repository's tokenizer.json, and pretraining uses subgraphs (default size 128). For downstream tasks the pretrained weights are loaded into a sequence classification model and fine-tuned, with MCC or F1 as the metric.

The fine-tuning code loads checkpoints named pretrain_params_epoch_N from a model directory, by default epoch 20. A result should record which Drive file and epoch it used and the repository commit; this page read commit 486343e5. The environment is old: Python 3.8, torch 1.7.1 with CUDA 11.0, and transformers 4.29.2.

profile.summary: DNAGPT is a GPT-style DNA language model from Tencent AI Lab and collaborators. It reads a DNA sequence, split into 6-letter words, and can also take numbers as input; it can generate new DNA sequence, classify a sequence or predict a numerical value such as mRNA expression level. Pre-training adds two side tasks, predicting whether a sequence was reversed and predicting its GC content, to the usual next-token prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv v3: author affiliations; arXiv abstract; README.md: Test examples; test.py get_model

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DNAGPT is a decoder-only Transformer: the 0.1B model has 12 blocks of unidirectional attention, 12 heads each and a hidden size of 768. The DNA sequence is cut into non-overlapping k-mers, and numbers are encoded as separate number tokens; each token type has its own embedding layer and output head. Pre-training combines three tasks: next-token prediction, GC-content prediction for a random segment, and prediction of whether the sequence order was flipped. Reversing sequences lets the left-to-right model use context from both directions. For a downstream task the needed heads are kept and the model is fine-tuned.
sections.source_locator: arXiv v3: Methods, Pre-training of DNAGPT; Section 3.1 Pre-training tasks; Figure 1 caption

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper describes four pre-trained variants: DNAGPT-H (0.1 billion parameters, human reference genome, 4096 tokens), DNAGPT-M (0.1 billion, reference genomes of 9 species, 4096 tokens), DNAGPT-S-512 (0.1 billion, all mammalian reference genomes, 512 tokens) and DNAGPT-B-512 (3 billion, all mammalian reference genomes, 512 tokens). The repository releases three foundation checkpoints, dna_gpt0.1b_h, dna_gpt0.1b_m and dna_gpt3b_m, plus two fine-tuned checkpoints: an expression-level regression model and an AATAAA genomic signal classification model. The README calls the 3B checkpoint multi-organism and does not map file names to the paper's variant names. A result should name the checkpoint file.

name: eccDNAMamba
description: Bidirectional Mamba state-space encoder for full-length extrachromosomal circular DNA up to 200 kb, trained with an augmentation that preserves circular topology.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: eccDNAMamba is a pretrained model for extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA), circular DNA molecules that carry amplified oncogenes in cancer. It reads full-length eccDNA sequences of 10 to 200 kbp, and copies the start of each sequence onto its end so the model sees across the point where the circle was opened. Fine-tuned versions are used for cancer-associated eccDNA prediction, copy-number level estimation, and telling real from pseudo-eccDNA.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; model card: Model Overview; inference_sample.py circular_augmentation

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: eccDNAMamba is a bidirectional state-space model: forward and reverse Mamba-2 encoders read the sequence in both directions, with cost linear in sequence length. DNA is tokenised by motif-level byte pair encoding (BPE) with a vocabulary of 4096. To respect the circular shape, a head-tail augmentation appends the first 64 tokens after the end of the sequence. The pretrained backbone is a masked language model (BiMambaForMaskedLM) with 24 layers and d_model 768. For classification, the published fine-tuning code mean-pools the hidden states and adds a two-layer classifier head.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model Overview; arXiv abstract; config.json; inference_sample.py

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The pretrained backbone is eccDNAMamba/eccDNAMamba-1M (read at revision 36d95a3f). Seven fine-tuned checkpoints are published under the same organisation: cancer eccDNA prediction (short and ultra-long), copy-number level prediction (thresholds 10 and 4.5) and real against pseudo-eccDNA for Arabidopsis thaliana, Gallus gallus and Homo sapiens. The fine-tuned ultra-long checkpoint names eccDNAMamba-1M as its base model. A result should name the checkpoint and its revision. The repository also has a pretraining entry point (main.py).

name: Evo
description: StripedHyena DNA language models of 7 billion parameters (Evo 1 and Evo 1.5), trained at single-nucleotide resolution on prokaryotic and phage genomes with 8 kb or 131 kb contexts, for zero-shot function prediction and sequence generation.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: Evo is a 7-billion-parameter DNA language model trained on prokaryotic whole genomes. It reads DNA one base at a time, with a context of 8,192 or 131,072 bases depending on the checkpoint, and predicts the next base. The developers use it to score how likely a sequence is and to generate new DNA, from single genes and CRISPR-Cas systems up to genome-scale sequences.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and checkpoint table; Usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Evo uses the StripedHyena architecture, a hybrid of multi-head attention and gated convolutions arranged in Hyena blocks. Hyena layers do most of the sequence processing and attention layers add targeted pattern recall, which gives near-linear scaling of compute and memory with context length. Tokens are single nucleotides (byte-level). The model is autoregressive: it outputs logits over the vocabulary at each position, which are used to sample new sequence or to score the log-likelihood of an existing one. Generation can run in a recurrent mode; the model card reports more than 500k bases generated on a single 80GB GPU.
sections.source_locator: README.md: introduction, Usage; model card: Model Architecture

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: evo-1-8k-base was pretrained at 8,192 context. evo-1-131k-base continues from it at 131,072 context. Evo 1.5 (evo-1.5-8k-base) extends the pretraining of evo-1-8k-base with 50% more data, to 450 billion tokens, and was introduced in a 2025 Nature paper. Two fine-tuned models generate CRISPR-Cas systems and IS200/IS605 transposons. The model card adds 15 intermediate pretraining checkpoints as branches. The Hugging Face weights had a projection-permutation bug that affects generation; the fix is loaded with revision="1.1_fix". The evo-model package had an inference bug in versions installed between Nov 15 and Dec 16, 2024, fixed from release 0.3. A result should name the checkpoint, the Hugging Face revision and the package version. The developers now point to Evo 2 as the successor.

strengths.text: Single-base resolution with a context of up to 131,072 bases in evo-1-131k-base, which the developers use to reason about and generate sequences at the genome scale.
Both scoring and generation scripts are provided, and the Evo 1.5 paper reports experimentally tested generated proteins and toxin-antitoxin systems (the authors' claim).
Code and weights are Apache-2.0 licensed and not gated, and intermediate pretraining checkpoints are released.

limitations.text: Trained on prokaryotic genomes only; the developers point to Evo 2 for all domains of life.
Needs a GPU that FlashAttention-2 supports, with pinned versions (FlashAttention up to 2.7.4.post0, PyTorch 2.7.x), plus custom StripedHyena kernels.
At 7 billion parameters it is large; the README example and scripts target a CUDA device. Exact GPU memory needs are not stated.
Known bugs affected earlier releases: the Hugging Face weights need revision 1.1_fix, and package versions installed between Nov 15 and Dec 16, 2024 must be upgraded.

name: GENERator
description: Generative transformer decoder DNA language models with 6-mer tokens, in eukaryote and prokaryote variants, that generate and embed long sequences (98 kb context in the first release, pretrained on 386 billion nucleotides of eukaryotic DNA).

profile.summary: GENERator is a family of generative DNA language models: it reads a DNA sequence and predicts what comes next, so it can both generate new sequence and produce embeddings for downstream tasks. The models are Transformer decoders that read DNA in 6-letter chunks (6-mers), with a context of up to 98k base pairs. The first release was trained on 386 billion nucleotides of eukaryotic DNA; a second release (GENERator-v2) adds eukaryote and prokaryote models.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GENERator is a decoder-only Transformer trained as a causal language model on DNA: it predicts the next token from the tokens before it. DNA is split into 6-mer tokens. The first-release 1.2B checkpoint uses a Llama-type configuration with 26 layers, hidden size 2048, 32 attention heads and 4 key-value heads, a vocabulary of 4128 tokens and up to 16384 token positions. Embeddings are read from the last hidden layer, either at the last token or averaged over all tokens. GENERator-v2 adds a training objective that recovers single-nucleotide likelihoods from k-mer tokens, and pretraining data concentrated on gene-centric and regulatory regions.

steps.shell:
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install flash-attn --no-build-isolation
steps.explanation: The README installs requirements with Python 3.10. It recommends FlashAttention for long pretraining; it is included here because the card's example loads the model with flash_attention_2.

steps.title: Load the model and generate
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "GenerTeam/GENERator-eukaryote-1.2b-base",
    attn_implementation="flash_attention_2",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
).cuda().eval()

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
    "GenerTeam/GENERator-eukaryote-1.2b-base",
    trust_remote_code=True,
)

sequences = [
    "ATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCG",
    "ACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGT"
]

processed_sequences = ["<s>" + seq[len(seq)%6:] for seq in sequences]

inputs = tokenizer(
    processed_sequences,
    add_special_tokens=False,
    return_tensors="pt",
    padding=True,
    padding_side="left",
).to("cuda")

with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=32, do_sample=False)

decoded_sequences = tokenizer.batch_decode(outputs, skip_special_tokens=True)
print(decoded_sequences)
PY

name: GenomeOcean

profile.summary: GenomeOcean is a family of generative DNA language models trained on co-assembled environmental metagenomes, mainly microbial DNA. It reads DNA split into multi-base tokens and predicts the next token. The developers provide scripts to produce sequence embeddings for analysis and to generate new DNA from a prompt. The largest model has 4 billion parameters and reads up to about 50,000 bases.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GenomeOcean is a decoder-only transformer trained by causal language modelling: it predicts the next token from the tokens before it. DNA is split by a BPE tokenizer with 4096 tokens, so 1024 tokens cover about 5,100 bp. The 4B checkpoint uses the Mistral architecture in transformers, with 24 layers, hidden size 3072, 12 attention heads and 4 key/value heads. The package uses vLLM for fast generation and also produces sequence embeddings. The developers report that the embeddings capture phylogenetic and protein-coding structure.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three base models are published: GenomeOcean-100M and GenomeOcean-500M with a 1024-token context, and GenomeOcean-4B with a 10240-token context. Two fine-tuned 4B models exist: GenomeOcean-4B-bgcFM, trained on 11M biosynthetic gene cluster sequences, and GenomeOcean-4B-Artificial-Detector, a classifier for GenomeOcean-generated sequences. The developers recommend the 4B model for general use. The package recently moved to the vLLM V1 engine and transformers 5.12 or later; under transformers 5, the tokenizer should be loaded with PreTrainedTokenizerFast. A result should name the checkpoint, its Hugging Face revision, and the package commit; this page read GenomeOcean-4B at revision 2bed2fc3 and the code at commit 06fa4331.

name: genomics-fm
description: Transformer encoder pretrained on unlabelled genomes with an ensemble of tokenisation vocabularies, then fine-tuned with a task-specific vocabulary for annotation, profile and variant effect prediction.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: Genomics-FM is a DNA foundation model meant to cut the amount of labelled data that genomic prediction tasks need. It is a BERT-style encoder pretrained on large amounts of unlabelled DNA with an ensemble of tokenisation vocabularies (BPE and 6-mer), then fine-tuned with one task-specific vocabulary on a small labelled set. The authors apply it to genome annotation, epigenomic and expression profile prediction, and variant effect assessment.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; srun_pretrain.py; srun_pretrain.sh

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is a BERT masked language model built on the MosaicML BERT code, which uses ALiBi position biases and FlashAttention. During pretraining each sequence is tokenised either with a BPE vocabulary or as 6-mers, and a prompt token marking the vocabulary ([BPE] or [KMER]) and the position scheme ([ALIBI] or [APE]) is put in front of it. Sequences are randomly replaced by their reverse complement half the time. Training masks tokens with a probability of 0.15 for BPE input and 0.15 divided by 6 for 6-mer input, over blocks of 512 tokens, for up to 1,000,000 steps in fp16. For a downstream task the model is fine-tuned with one chosen vocabulary.

name: GROVER
description: BERT-style DNA language model trained on the human genome with a byte-pair vocabulary chosen to carry the most sequence information, whose embeddings are fine-tuned for tasks such as promoter and protein-DNA binding prediction.

profile.summary: GROVER is a DNA language model pretrained on the human genome. It splits DNA into variable-length tokens learned by byte-pair encoding, and turns a DNA sequence into contextual embeddings. Its authors intend it as a foundation model that is fine-tuned for a specific task, such as promoter identity or protein-DNA binding.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; tutorial notebook, Overview

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GROVER is a BERT model for masked language modelling: 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads and a vocabulary of 609 tokens. The vocabulary comes from byte-pair encoding of the human genome, and the authors chose the vocabulary size with a next-k-mer prediction task. Because byte-pair tokens depend on the surrounding sequence, a short sequence can be tokenised differently from the same stretch in the whole genome; the card advises adding 100 nucleotides at each end. For a task, the pretrained model is loaded with a classification head and fine-tuned on labelled sequences.

run_guide.summary: Load the pretrained GROVER checkpoint from Hugging Face, then fine-tune it to classify CTCF binding sites as in the authors' tutorial.
prerequisites: Python with PyTorch, transformers, pandas, NumPy and scikit-learn. The sources do not give versions or an install command for these; the tutorial was written for Google Colab, where they are preinstalled.
A GPU for fine-tuning: the tutorial calls it necessary and uses a Colab T4.
Internet access to download the checkpoint from Hugging Face and the example CTCF dataset from datashare.tu-dresden.de.

steps.title: Fine-tune on the CTCF example and evaluate
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
import wget
import os
import numpy as np

from sklearn.metrics import matthews_corrcoef, accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

import transformers
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, Trainer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification, TrainingArguments
from torch.utils.data import Dataset

CTCF_dataset_url = "https://datashare.tu-dresden.de/s/pjb5gcWGGrbcARN/download/CTCF_dataset.tsv"
file_name = "CTCF_dataset.tsv"
if os.path.exists(file_name):
  os.remove(file_name) # if exists, remove it directly
file_name = wget.download(CTCF_dataset_url, out=file_name)

CTCF_dataset = pd.read_csv('CTCF_dataset.tsv', sep='\t')
train = CTCF_dataset.sample(frac=0.8, random_state=0)
validation = CTCF_dataset.drop(train.index)
test = validation.sample(frac=0.5, random_state=0)
validation = validation.drop(test.index)
train = train.reset_index(drop=True)
validation = validation.reset_index(drop=True)
test = test.reset_index(drop=True)

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("PoetschLab/GROVER")
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("PoetschLab/GROVER")

class SupervisedDataset(Dataset):
    """Dataset for supervised fine-tuning."""
    def __init__(self, texts, labels, tokenizer):
        super(SupervisedDataset, self).__init__()
        sequences = [text for text in texts]
        output = tokenizer(
            sequences,
            add_special_tokens=True,
            max_length=310,
            padding="longest",
            return_tensors="pt",
            truncation=True
        )
        self.input_ids = output["input_ids"]
        self.attention_mask = output["attention_mask"]
        self.labels = labels
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.input_ids)
    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return dict(
            input_ids=self.input_ids[i],
            labels=self.labels[i],
            attention_mask=self.attention_mask[i]
        )

train_dataset = SupervisedDataset(train.sequence, train.label, tokenizer)
test_dataset = SupervisedDataset(test.sequence, test.label, tokenizer)
val_dataset = SupervisedDataset(validation.sequence, validation.label, tokenizer)

def calculate_metric_with_sklearn(logits: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray):
    predictions = np.argmax(logits, axis=-1)
    return {
        "accuracy": accuracy_score(labels, predictions),
        "f1": f1_score(labels, predictions, average="macro", zero_division=0),
        "matthews_correlation": matthews_corrcoef(labels, predictions),
        "precision": precision_score(labels, predictions, average="macro", zero_division=0),
        "recall": recall_score(labels, predictions, average="macro", zero_division=0),
    }

def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    logits, labels = eval_pred
    if isinstance(logits, tuple):  # Unpack logits if it's a tuple
        logits = logits[0]
    return calculate_metric_with_sklearn(logits, labels)

train_args = TrainingArguments(seed = 42,
                               output_dir=".",
                               per_device_train_batch_size=16,
                               eval_strategy="epoch",
                               learning_rate=0.000001,
                               num_train_epochs=4
                               )
trainer = transformers.Trainer(
                                model=model,
                                tokenizer=tokenizer,
                                compute_metrics=compute_metrics,
                                train_dataset=train_dataset,
                                eval_dataset=val_dataset,
                                args = train_args
                                )
trainer.train()
results = trainer.evaluate(eval_dataset=test_dataset)
print(results)
PY

name: JanusDNA
description: Hybrid Mamba, attention and mixture-of-experts DNA model that combines autoregressive and masked pretraining to read sequences of up to 1 Mb in both directions at single-nucleotide resolution.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: JanusDNA is a DNA language model that reads sequence one nucleotide at a time and is designed for long inputs. It is pre-trained on the human reference genome so that each position is predicted from the sequence on both sides of it, and its learned representations are then fine-tuned for tasks such as regulatory element classification and eQTL prediction. The models are small: the README lists sizes of 1.980M to 2.009M and 7.662M parameters.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; arXiv v4: Section 4.1, Table 9; README.md: Reproducing Experiments

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The input sequence is encoded by two independent stacks, one reading left to right and one right to left. Each stack has 8 layers, each with a Mamba block and a feed-forward block, and half of the feed-forward blocks are replaced by mixture-of-experts blocks with 16 experts. A final fusion layer, a FlexAttention layer with 4 heads, joins the two directions with an attention mask that lets the prediction for a position see the left context from the forward pass and the right context from the backward pass, but not the position itself. This lets every token contribute to the loss, as in autoregressive training, while the model still learns from both sides, as in masked training. One variant also replaces the Mamba block in the fifth layer with a causal attention layer (mid-attention). A later update adds two MLP layers after the fusion layer.
sections.source_locator: arXiv v4: Section 3.1; Appendix B.2.1 Architecture configuration; README.md: Update 2025-08-01

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper pre-trains three widths: hidden size 32 and 72 for 1,024-nucleotide inputs (10,000 steps), and 144 for 131,072-nucleotide inputs (50,000 steps). The 32 and 72 widths come with and without mid-attention. The weights dataset on Harvard Dataverse (version 2) holds five original checkpoints with their configuration files and five later checkpoints with the final MLP layers (JanusDNA_mlp), which the README calls the latest. The GenomicBenchmarks script expects a pretrained checkpoint under outputs/pretrain/hg38/, in a folder named after its configuration. A result should give the width, the input length, whether mid-attention was used and whether the final MLP was used.
sections.source_locator: arXiv v4: Appendix B.2.1 Pre-training setup; Dataverse file list; README.md: Update

sections.title: Setting up the code
sections.body: The README covers environment setup and scripts that reproduce the paper: pre-training on hg38 and fine-tuning on GenomicBenchmarks, the Nucleotide Transformer tasks and the DNALongBench eQTL tasks. Setup uses a conda environment file and a prebuilt Mamba wheel for CUDA 12, PyTorch 2.5 and Python 3.11 on Linux x86_64. The scripts contain placeholder paths to fill in, and the GenomicBenchmarks script is written for 8 GPUs. The README gives no example of loading a checkpoint and embedding a single sequence.

name: LucaOne
description: Transformer encoder pretrained jointly on nucleic acid and protein sequences from about 170,000 species, giving one representation for DNA, RNA and protein inputs.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: LucaOne is a biological foundation model that reads nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) and protein sequences with one shared model. Given a sequence and its type, it returns an embedding: a matrix with one vector per residue or a single vector for the whole sequence. These embeddings are used as inputs to downstream models for sequence-level or residue-level classification and regression.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: title, TimeLine 2025/12/31; LucaOneApp README: embedding methods and parameters

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LucaOne (also called LucaGPLM) is a transformer encoder over a joint vocabulary of nucleotides and amino acids. The published checkpoint has a masked language model head, which the developers describe as for pre-training and sequence recovery; the full set of pretraining tasks is described in the paper, which was not read. The published default checkpoint has 20 layers, hidden size 2560, 40 attention heads and a 39-token vocabulary, with no absolute position embeddings. Each input is marked as gene (DNA or RNA) or prot. The output is the last hidden layer: per-token vectors including [CLS] and [SEP], which can be pooled to one vector by mean, [CLS] or trainable attention pooling. Long sequences are split into overlapping fragments and the embeddings merged.
sections.source_locator: model card: Usage; config.json; LucaOneApp README: embedding methods, notes

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Checkpoints are named by training step. The README recommends lucaone at step 36000000, 17600000 or 5600000 for both nucleic acid and protein, lucaone-gene at step 36800000 for DNA and RNA only, and lucaone-prot at step 30000000 for protein only. The original code downloads them from the developers' FTP server by --llm_type, --llm_version and --llm_step. Since 2025 they are also on Hugging Face under LucaGroup, loaded with the lucaone package (version 1.1.1 for the card read). A result should name the checkpoint and step, the route (FTP code or Hugging Face) and the Hugging Face revision; this page read LucaOne-default-step36M at revision f0d2807e.
