steps.title: Embed a nucleotide sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import lucaone
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel, TrainingArguments, Trainer

# model_id
model_id = "LucaGroup/LucaOne-default-step36M"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    trust_remote_code=True,
    force_download=True
)

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    task_level="token_level",
    task_type="embedding",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    force_download=True
)

# device
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model.to(device)
model.eval()

# nucleotide sequence
nucleotide_sequence = "ATGCGTACGTTAGC"
nucleotide_inputs = tokenizer(
    nucleotide_sequence,
    # note: gene sequence(for DNA or RNA), seq_type must be 'gene'
    seq_type="gene",
    return_tensors="pt",
    add_special_tokens=True
)
new_nucleotide_inputs = {}
for item in nucleotide_inputs.items():
    new_nucleotide_inputs[item[0]] = item[1].to(device)
nucleotide_inputs = new_nucleotide_inputs

with torch.no_grad():
    nucleotide_outputs = model(**nucleotide_inputs)
    # last hidden matrix as embedding matrix: [batch_size, seq_len + 2, hidden_size]
    nucleotide_last_hidden = nucleotide_outputs.last_hidden_state
    # mean pooling
    mean_nucleotide_embedding = nucleotide_last_hidden[:, 1:-1, :].mean(dim=1)
print(f"Nucleotide Embedding Shape: {nucleotide_last_hidden.shape}")
print(mean_nucleotide_embedding)
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's feature-extraction example, wrapped in a shell heredoc and shortened: the protein half and some intermediate print lines are left out. Use seq_type="prot" for a protein sequence, as the card shows.

outputs: The shape of the embedding matrix, [batch_size, seq_len + 2, hidden_size], and the mean-pooled embedding vector.

name: MutBERT
description: Masked DNA language model that represents the human genome as allele-frequency distributions from population data, so pretraining concentrates on sites of variation.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: MutBERT is a DNA language model for the human genome that is built to learn from genetic variation such as single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Instead of training on one reference sequence, it encodes each genome position as a probability over the four bases, taken from allele frequencies in the 1000 Genomes Project. Given a DNA sequence, it outputs per-nucleotide embeddings that can be pooled into a sequence embedding or fine-tuned for classification.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; 2.2 Probabilistic genome representation; README: 4.2 Get the embeddings

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MutBERT is a transformer encoder trained with masked language modelling. It has 12 encoder layers and uses rotary position embeddings (RoPE) and flash attention. Each position in the input is a distribution over the bases: positions without observed variants give the reference base a probability of 1, and variable positions carry the observed allele frequencies. Because the input is a probability matrix and not a token sequence, the usual embedding look-up is replaced by a linear layer, so each position's embedding is a weighted sum of the base embeddings. During pretraining the authors apply temperature scaling to the skewed allele probabilities. The model works at single-nucleotide level with a vocabulary of A, T, C, G and five special tokens. In the README usage example, plain sequences are passed as a one-hot matrix.
sections.source_locator: Paper: 2.1 Model architecture, 2.2 Probabilistic genome representation, 2.3 Tokenization and vocabulary, 2.4; README: 4.2 Get the embeddings

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three pretrained checkpoints share one architecture and differ only in the training data. MutBERT uses probabilistic genomes from the 1000 Genomes Project. MutBERT-Multi uses probabilistic genomes from a 100-species whole-genome alignment. MutBERT-Ref (on Hugging Face, CompBioDSA/MutBERT-Human-Ref) takes one-hot encodings of the hg38 reference and serves as the deterministic baseline. All were trained for 120 000 steps with batch size 2048 and maximum sequence length 512. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; this page read MutBERT at a6cdc94d, MutBERT-Human-Ref at 766be54e and MutBERT-Multi at cbdab668.
sections.source_locator: Paper: 2.1 Model architecture, 2.4 to 2.5; README: 2. Model and Results; model cards: title lines

sections.title: Evaluation in the paper
sections.body: The authors compared MutBERT with DNABERT-2, several Nucleotide Transformer versions and modified MutBERT variants on transcription factor binding sites (from the GUE benchmark), the Nucleotide Transformer downstream tasks and eQTL variant effect prediction. For the eQTL task they extended MutBERT's input from 512 to 2048 base pairs and trained an SVM on the embeddings. The authors report that MutBERT ranked among the top models, and that it beat the alternatives in most of the three eQTL distance categories. They note it was pretrained on 4 L20 GPUs for 6 days.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; 2.7 Downstream tasks; 3.2 eQTL variant effect prediction; Discussion; README: 6. Finetune

steps.title: Compute an embedding
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel

model_name = "CompBioDSA/MutBERT"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(model_name, trust_remote_code=True)

dna = "ATCGGGGCCCATTA"
inputs = tokenizer(dna, return_tensors='pt')["input_ids"]

mut_inputs = F.one_hot(inputs, num_classes=len(tokenizer)).float().to("cpu")  # len(tokenizer) is vocab size
last_hidden_state = model(mut_inputs).last_hidden_state   # [1, sequence_length, 768]

# embedding with mean pooling
embedding_mean = torch.mean(last_hidden_state[0], dim=0)
print(embedding_mean.shape) # expect to be 768

# embedding with max pooling
embedding_max = torch.max(last_hidden_state[0], dim=0)[0]
print(embedding_max.shape) # expect to be 768
PY

name: OmniNA
description: Generative nucleotide model pretrained on 91.7 million sequences with their text annotations from many species, fine-tuned to answer sequence tasks in natural language.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

profile.summary: OmniNA is a generative foundation model for nucleotide sequences from many species. It was pretrained on 91.7 million DNA and RNA sequences from the NCBI nucleotide database, each paired with its text annotation, so that it learns to write an annotation for a sequence. After fine-tuning, it answers questions about an input sequence in natural language, for example whether it is a promoter, or which species it comes from.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Data processing for OmniNA pre-training; README: Overview, Prepare Data

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: OmniNA uses the LLaMA architecture, an auto-regressive decoder-only transformer. Sequences and annotations share one byte pair encoding tokenizer, built with SentencePiece and trained on nucleotide sequences and wiki-103 text, with 32,001 tokens. Each pretraining example is a prompt with three parts: an instruction, a nucleotide sequence and its annotation, and the model is trained to generate the text. Inputs are capped at 601 tokens. Fine-tuning casts each downstream task as a question and answer: the training file adds a question column, and the model learns to generate the answer.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model architecture and pre-training; Data processing; Figure 1 caption; README: Prepare Data

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper and README describe three sizes. The README table gives OmniNA-66M (8 layers, 8 heads, 66 million parameters), OmniNA-330M (16 layers, 16 heads, 330 million) and OmniNA-1.7B (24 layers, 32 heads, 1.7 billion). Hugging Face holds XLS/OmniNA-66m, XLS/OmniNA-220m and XLS/OmniNA-1.7B. The XLS/OmniNA-220m configuration has 16 layers and 16 heads, the shape the README gives for OmniNA-330M, so the middle checkpoint appears to be the same model under two different size names. The model card read (1.7B) holds only a licence tag. A result should name the Hugging Face checkpoint and revision; this page read 66m at 2c5e876a, 220m at 64ea6ce7 and 1.7B at 73d208a3.
sections.source_locator: README: Model Variants, Installation; config.json of each checkpoint; Hugging Face listing; Paper: Results

sections.title: Evaluation in the paper
sections.body: The authors fine-tuned OmniNA on 17 tasks covering sequence detection (taxonomy classification through genomic element detection) and species classification, and report that OmniNA-1.7B surpasses or rivals the compared methods. They also apply it to the effect of mutations on DNA and RNA processing. The authors themselves warn that test sets may overlap the training data of the compared models, and that converting regression baselines to classification may bias the comparison.

name: PlantCaduceus
description: Caduceus and Mamba DNA language model pretrained on 16 angiosperm genomes, fine-tuned to predict translation start and stop sites and splice sites across plant species and to score deleterious variants.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: PlantCaduceus (short name PlantCAD) is a DNA language model for flowering plants, pretrained on the genomes of 16 angiosperm species. It reads 512-bp DNA windows one nucleotide at a time, looking at both strands. Its embeddings feed small classifiers that predict translation start and stop sites and splice sites in species it was not trained on, and its masked-base likelihoods give a zero-shot score for how deleterious a single-nucleotide variant is.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: PlantCAD overview; Paper: Abstract, Introduction, Fig. 1 caption

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PlantCaduceus uses the Caduceus architecture, which builds on the Mamba state-space sequence model and adds bi-directionality and reverse complement (RC) equivariance, so both DNA strands are modelled together. It uses single-nucleotide tokens. Pretraining is masked language modelling: 15% of positions in each 512-bp window are masked and the model is trained with cross-entropy loss on them. Following GPN, the pretraining set down-samples noncoding regions and down-weights repeats. Downstream, frozen embeddings train XGBoost or linear classifiers, and the zero-shot score is the log-likelihood difference between the reference and alternate allele at a masked position.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Fig. 1 caption; Results; Methods; README: PlantCAD overview

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: PlantCAD comes in four sizes, named by their number of Caduceus blocks: PlantCaduceus_l20, l24, l28 and l32, all with a 512-bp input. The model card recommends the largest, l32, for zero-shot scoring. The same repository now also hosts PlantCAD2, a later generation with an 8192-bp input and separate checkpoints (Small, Medium, Large); it is a different model and is not covered here. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; the listing read on 2026-11-26 gives l32 at e624c13c, l28 at 5ac1d5e7, l24 at 8c41e4d5 and l20 at d1b3c7d4.
sections.source_locator: README: Model summary; model card: Model Overview; Hugging Face listing; Paper: Results, Table 1

sections.title: Evaluation in the paper
sections.body: The authors trained XGBoost and linear classifiers on Arabidopsis labels for translation initiation and termination sites and splice donor and acceptor sites, then tested them on species in the pretraining set (Oryza sativa, Sorghum bicolor) and outside it (Gossypium hirsutum, Glycine max, Zea mays). They compared PlantCaduceus with other DNA language models including GPN and AgroNT. For variants, they compared zero-shot scores with phyloP, phastCons, GPN and AgroNT. The claim of best cross-species performance is the authors'.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; README: PlantCAD overview

steps.title: Compute embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForMaskedLM

device = 'cuda:0'
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('kuleshov-group/PlantCaduceus_l32')
model = AutoModelForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    'kuleshov-group/PlantCaduceus_l32', trust_remote_code=True
).to(device)

sequence = ""

input_ids = tokenizer.encode_plus(
    sequence, return_tensors="pt", return_attention_mask=False,
    return_token_type_ids=False
)["input_ids"].to(device)

with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model(input_ids=input_ids, output_hidden_states=True)

embeddings = outputs.hidden_states[-1].to(torch.float32).cpu().numpy()

# Average forward and reverse complement embeddings
hidden_size = embeddings.shape[-1] // 2
forward = embeddings[..., 0:hidden_size]
reverse = embeddings[..., hidden_size:][:, ::-1, :]
averaged_embeddings = (forward + reverse) / 2
print(averaged_embeddings.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README 'Quick example' wrapped in a shell heredoc. It downloads PlantCaduceus_l32, runs one 512-bp sequence on the GPU and averages the forward and reverse-complement halves of the last hidden state.

outputs: The shape of the strand-averaged embedding array: one row per token of the input sequence, with half the width of the raw hidden state. The README does not print the expected numbers.

name: SPACE
description: Supervised DNA model that learns sequence representations by predicting genomic profiles such as chromatin accessibility across species, using species- and profile-specific mixture-of-experts layers.

version.note: Family record; checkpoints are on configurations

attributes.provenance_note: Listed on the GENEB leaderboard as a genomic foundation model family.

profile.summary: SPACE is a DNA model that learns sequence representations by supervised training rather than by masked or next-token prediction. It is trained to predict thousands of genomic profiles, such as chromatin accessibility, transcription factor binding, histone marks and CAGE, from long human and mouse DNA sequences. Its encoder can then be fine-tuned or used as a feature extractor for other DNA tasks, and the full model predicts the profiles themselves.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; 4.1 Pre-training; README: Try the Genomic Profile Prediction, Downstream Tasks

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SPACE (Species-Profile Adaptive Collaborative Experts) keeps the Enformer setup of predicting genomic profiles from DNA, and adds two Mixture of Experts (MoE) parts. A species-aware encoder adds a trainable species embedding and routes each input sparsely across experts, so it can learn both species-specific and shared features. A profile-grouped enhancement decoder uses gated experts to model dependencies between profile types before the human and mouse output heads. The implementation is based on Enformer-Pytorch and Mod-Squad. In the released configuration the input is 131,072 bp, the model width is 1536 with 11 layers and 8 attention heads, the species MoE has 4 experts and the profile MoE has 8, and topk is set to 3.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; 3 Method; README: Acknowledgments; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README names one pretrained checkpoint, yangyz1230/space on Hugging Face, which appears to be the paper's SPACE (large). Smaller variants in the paper (hidden size 768) were built only for ablation studies, and the README names none of them. The training data are the Enformer human and mouse sets, which the authors converted from the Basenji TensorFlow files to H5 and published as the Hugging Face dataset yangyz1230/space. A result should name the checkpoint revision; this page read revision 63c9f501.
sections.source_locator: README: Pre-trained Model, Dataset; Paper: Appendix H; Hugging Face API response

sections.title: Evaluation in the paper
sections.body: The authors fine-tuned the encoder on the Nucleotide Transformer downstream tasks, where they report the best result on 11 of 18 tasks, including against the 2.5B-parameter NT-Multispecies model, and they compare with Enformer on the GUE benchmark. With frozen embeddings on the BEND benchmark they report strong results on chromatin accessibility, histone modification and CpG methylation, but limited effectiveness on the two variant effect tasks. These are the authors' own results.

profile.summary: AIDO.DNA, now renamed GB.DNA by its developer GenBio AI, is a large DNA language model meant as a general-purpose encoder of DNA sequence. It reads up to 4,000 nucleotides one base at a time and was pretrained on 10.6 billion nucleotides from 796 species. Its embeddings are fine-tuned or probed for tasks such as gene expression prediction, genome mining, in silico mutagenesis and sequence generation.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; model card: introduction, Tokenization; ModelGenerator backbones: deprecated aliases

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: AIDO.DNA is a BERT-style, encoder-only dense transformer trained with masked language modelling. It uses single-nucleotide tokens from a 5-letter vocabulary (A, T, C, G, N), with a [CLS] token at the start and an [EOS] token at the end of each sequence. The authors updated the BERT design with SwiGLU, LayerNorms and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE). The 7B model has 32 layers, 32 attention heads and hidden size 4352. Its design bet, in the authors' words, is to scale model size while keeping a short 4k context. It was trained for 100000 iterations at global batch size 1024 on 256 H100 GPUs with Megatron-LM, which took 8 days.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model Architectural Details, Tokenization, Training Details; bioRxiv abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two pretrained checkpoints are released: a 7B model and a 300M model. Both were first published as AIDO.DNA-7B and AIDO.DNA-300M and are now named GB.DNA-7B and GB.DNA-300M on Hugging Face; the old names still resolve to the new repositories. In ModelGenerator the backbones are gb_dna_7b and gb_dna_300m, and the old names aido_dna_7b and aido_dna_300m remain as deprecated aliases. The 300M card gives no training details of its own and refers to the 7B card. A result should name the checkpoint and its revision; this page read GB.DNA-7B at 5dd948f7 and GB.DNA-300M at a833c560.
sections.source_locator: Hugging Face API responses (requested by old name); ModelGenerator backbones; 300M model card

sections.title: Evaluation in the paper
sections.body: The authors evaluated the 7B model on supervised, generative and zero-shot tasks in functional genomics, synthetic biology and drug development, choosing hyperparameters on a 10% validation split. They report that it outperforms earlier encoder-only DNA models without using new data, and argue that new scaling laws are needed for compute-optimal DNA language models. These are the authors' claims; only the abstract and model card were read.

steps.title: Compute embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from modelgenerator.tasks import Embed
model = Embed.from_config({"model.backbone": "gb_dna_300m"}).eval()

profile.summary: Nucleotide Transformer v3 (NTv3) is a family of DNA models from InstaDeep that read up to about 1 million bases at single-base resolution, across many species. Pre-trained checkpoints learn from unlabelled genomes by predicting masked bases and give embeddings. Post-trained checkpoints are further trained to predict functional genomics tracks (such as chromatin accessibility, histone marks and transcription factor binding) and genome annotations, given the species.
profile.summary_source_locator: docs/nucleotide_transformer_v3.md at commit 2dc37b86: opening, Model Variants and Sizes, How to Use

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: NTv3 is a U-Net. A convolutional tower shortens the single-base token sequence by 2 to the power of the number of downsampling blocks (128 for the main models, which have 7), a transformer processes the compressed sequence with self-attention, and a deconvolutional tower with skip connections restores single-base resolution. Pre-training uses masked language modelling on 9 trillion base pairs from OpenGenome2, with a length curriculum up to 1 Mb. Post-training adds supervised learning on about 16,000 functional tracks and annotation labels from 24 species, with adaptive layer norms for species conditioning. Post-trained track and annotation outputs cover the middle 37.5% of the input.
sections.source_locator: docs at commit 2dc37b86: Architecture, Training Overview, Ablations note, How to Use

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The initial release (2025) has pre-trained models of 8M, 100M and 650M parameters and post-trained models of 100M and 650M, plus intermediate checkpoints (8kb and 131kb stages) and experimental 5-downsample models of 592M. Each repository is tagged v1.0. These checkpoints need the code at commit 2dc37b8. InstaDeep has since released a second generation (NTv3_pretrained, NTv3_tracks, NTv3_tracks_1mb, NTv3_annot_mammals, _plants, _insects) with a different architecture, which the current code loads instead; the initial-release checkpoints are unchanged and still published. name: PhyloGPN
description: Phylogenetic genomic language model (PhyloGPN).

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: PhyloGPN is a convolutional network that reads DNA sequence alone and outputs, for every position, the parameters of a nucleotide substitution model (Felsenstein's F81). It was trained to fit those parameters to columns of the Zoonomia multispecies whole-genome alignment given a phylogenetic tree, which makes the output a statement about how constrained each site is. It needs no alignment at prediction time, so it can score variants and supply embeddings from a single sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: docs/models/phylogpn.md opening paragraph; model card first paragraph; arXiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The network is convolutional: 20 stacks of 2 layers with kernel size 5, inner dimension 480 and outer dimension 960, and a receptive field of 481 positions. It is trained to maximise the likelihood of each alignment column under a phylogenetic tree: the output at a position gives the F81 rate parameters for that site, and the stationary distribution of that substitution process says how viable each allele is there. Because the tree and alignment enter only through the loss, prediction takes plain sequence. The model works as a sliding window: an input of length l yields outputs for the l minus 480 central positions, so sequences are padded before scoring.
sections.source_locator: config.json; model card first and third paragraphs; docs/models/phylogpn.md

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility

It is one of four model families in the songlab-cal/gpn package, which supports PhyloGPN for inference only, not training or fine-tuning, and reaches it through AutoClass APIs rather than the gpn command line. The checkpoint ships its own modelling code, so loading needs trust_remote_code. A result should name the checkpoint revision, the padding used and the window conventions.

steps.title: Score a batch of sequences
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

checkpoint = "songlab/PhyloGPN"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(checkpoint, trust_remote_code=True)

# Example data
seqs = [
    "TATAAA",
    "GGCCAATCT",
    "CACGTG",
    "AGGTCACGT",
    "GCCAGCC",
    "GGGGATTTCC"
]

# Output length is input length minus 480 (the receptive field size minus 1)
pad_token = tokenizer.pad_token
pad_size = 481 // 2
pad_sequence = lambda seq: pad_token * pad_size + seq + pad_token * pad_size
padded_seqs = [pad_sequence(seq) for seq in seqs]
input_tensor = tokenizer(padded_seqs, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)["input_ids"]

with torch.no_grad():
    padded_embeddings = model.get_embeddings(input_tensor)
    padded_logits = model(input_tensor) # These are log rate parameters for the F81 model

embeddings = []
logits = []

for i in range(len(seqs)):
    length = len(seqs[i])
    embeddings.append(padded_embeddings[i, :length])
    logits.append({})

    for k in "ACGT":
        logits[-1][k] = padded_logits[k][i, :length]

print(embeddings[0].shape, {k: v.shape for k, v in logits[0].items()})
PY

name: BPNet
description: BPNet convolutional architecture trained from scratch per task.

version.note: Family record; variants are on configurations

profile.summary: BPNet is a convolutional neural network that predicts transcription-factor binding from DNA sequence at single-base resolution. It reads a stretch of genomic sequence and predicts the strand-specific read profile and the total read count of a ChIP-nexus or ChIP-seq experiment over that region. It is not a pretrained model: users train a new BPNet on their own experiment, then interpret it to find the sequence motifs that drive binding.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README.md opening paragraph

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: In the paper, the body of the network is a first convolutional layer of 64 filters of width 25 bp, followed by 9 dilated convolutional layers of 64 filters of width 3, with the dilation rate doubling at every layer and no pooling, so base resolution is kept. Two output heads per transcription factor sit on top: a deconvolutional layer that predicts the probability of a read at each position on each strand (profile shape), and a global average pooling layer with a fully connected layer that predicts the total read count. The loss is a multinomial negative log-likelihood for profile shape plus a mean squared error on log total counts. A control track is given as an extra input so that experimental bias is regressed out. After training, contribution scores and TF-MoDISco are used to extract motifs.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, 'BPNet predicts TF binding profiles from sequence'; Methods, BPNet architecture and loss function

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are two generations of the code in the same repository. The original package that accompanied the paper is kept at the v0-final tag; it uses a `bpnet train` command, a dataspec.yml file and Python 3.6 with TensorFlow 1. The current master branch is described by its authors as the improved version and the one to use; it has separate `bpnet-train`, `bpnet-predict` and `bpnet-shap` commands, Python 3.7, and an example configuration with a 2114 bp input, a 1000 bp output profile, a first filter of width 21 and 8 dilated layers. The two generations use different defaults, so a result should name the code version (tag or commit), the architecture parameters file and the training data. The trained mouse ESC model from the paper (Oct4, Sox2, Nanog, Klf4) is published on Zenodo and on Kipoi as BPNet-OSKN.

strengths.text: Predicts binding at single-base resolution, because the network uses no pooling and models the full read profile on each strand.
The package covers the whole path from training to interpretation: prediction tracks, per-base contribution scores, and motif discovery with TF-MoDISco and motif hit calling with FiNeMo.
Code is MIT licensed, and the trained paper model is on Zenodo under CC-BY-4.0.

limitations.text: There is no general pretrained model. Each use needs a new model trained on aligned reads from a specific experiment, plus peak calls, a reference genome and preprocessing with samtools, bedtools and bedGraphToBigWig.
The developers recommend a GPU with NVIDIA drivers and CUDA for training.

The current package differs from the version in the paper (commands, defaults and environment), and the README says a preprint for the new version is not yet out, so results from the two are not directly comparable.

limitations.text: The current environment pins an old Python (3.7), and the original package needs Python 3.6 and TensorFlow 1.

run_guide.summary: Install the current BPNet package, train a model on one prepared ChIP-seq experiment and predict profiles on held-out chromosomes.
prerequisites: A machine with an NVIDIA GPU, drivers and CUDA is recommended for training.
Miniconda, used to create a Python 3.7 environment.

Prepared data for one experiment: plus and minus strand signal bigWigs, a filtered peaks BED file, optional control bigWigs and GC-matched background regions, hg38 reference FASTA, chromosome sizes and a chroms.txt list. The README points to wiki pages for these steps (Download-test-data, Preprocessing, Outlier_removal, Background_generation).
input_data.json, bpnet_params.json and splits.json written as in the README tutorial.

steps.title: Create the environment
steps.shell:
conda create --name bpnet python=3.7
conda activate bpnet
steps.explanation: Creates and activates a Python 3.7 conda environment.

steps.title: Install BPNet and helper tools
steps.shell:
pip install git+https://github.com/kundajelab/bpnet.git
conda install -y -c bioconda samtools=1.1 bedtools ucsc-bedgraphtobigwig
steps.explanation: Installs the package from the repository's default branch, which may be newer than the commit read here, and the tools used to build bigWig tracks.

steps.title: Choose the counts loss weight
steps.shell: bpnet-counts-loss-weight --input-data input_data.json
steps.explanation: Computes the counts loss weight to put in the loss_weights field of bpnet_params.json.

steps.title: Train
steps.shell:
BASE_DIR=ENCSR000EGM
DATA_DIR=$BASE_DIR/data
MODEL_DIR=$BASE_DIR/models
REFERENCE_DIR=reference
CHROM_SIZES=$REFERENCE_DIR/hg38.chrom.sizes
REFERENCE_GENOME=$REFERENCE_DIR/hg38.genome.fa
CV_SPLITS=$BASE_DIR/splits.json
INPUT_DATA=$BASE_DIR/input_data.json
MODEL_PARAMS=$BASE_DIR/bpnet_params.json

mkdir $MODEL_DIR
bpnet-train \
        --input-data $INPUT_DATA \
        --output-dir $MODEL_DIR \
        --reference-genome $REFERENCE_GENOME \
        --chroms $(paste -s -d ' ' $REFERENCE_DIR/chroms.txt) \
        --chrom-sizes $CHROM_SIZES \
        --splits $CV_SPLITS \
        --model-arch-name BPNet \
        --model-arch-params-json $MODEL_PARAMS \
        --sequence-generator-name BPNet \
        --model-output-filename model \
        --input-seq-len 2114 \
        --output-len 1000 \
        --shuffle \
        --threads 10 \
        --epochs 100 \
        --batch-size 64 \
        --reverse-complement-augmentation \
        --early-stopping-patience 10 \
        --reduce-lr-on-plateau-patience 5 \
        --learning-rate 0.001
steps.explanation: The README's training command for the ENCODE CTCF example ENCSR000EGM. The README notes training may take a few minutes to start.

steps.title: Predict on the test chromosomes
steps.shell:
PREDICTIONS_DIR=$BASE_DIR/predictions_and_metrics
mkdir $PREDICTIONS_DIR
bpnet-predict \
        --model $MODEL_DIR/model_split000 \
        --chrom-sizes $CHROM_SIZES \
        --chroms chr7 chr13 chr17 chr19 chr21 chrX \
        --test-indices-file None \
        --reference-genome $REFERENCE_GENOME \
        --output-dir $PREDICTIONS_DIR \
        --input-data $INPUT_DATA \
        --sequence-generator-name BPNet \
        --input-seq-len 2114 \
        --output-len 1000 \
        --output-window-size 1000 \
        --batch-size 64 \
        --reverse-complement-average \
        --threads 2 \
        --generate-predicted-profile-bigWigs
steps.explanation: Runs the trained model on the held-out chromosomes from splits.json, in the same shell as the training step so the variables are set.

outputs: Test-set metrics in the predictions_and_metrics directory, and predicted profile bigWig tracks because --generate-predicted-profile-bigWigs is given.

profile.summary: Genos is a family of DNA language models for the human genome from the Genos Team in Hangzhou, China (GitHub and Hugging Face organisation BGI-HangzhouAI). It reads DNA one base at a time, with inputs of up to about one million bases, and is trained to predict the next base. Its internal representations (embeddings) are used for tasks such as classifying genomic elements, predicting variant effects and, after fine-tuning, predicting RNA-seq coverage from DNA sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Methods; README_en.md: Model Architecture, Notebook Usage Examples

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Genos is a decoder-style Transformer with a mixture-of-experts feed-forward layer. Each base (A, T, C, G or N) is one token. Every layer has grouped-query attention, with 16 heads sharing 8 key-value groups, and rotary position embeddings for long contexts; a router sends each token to 2 of 8 expert networks. A final linear layer gives the probability of the next base, which is the training objective. Pre-training mixed sequence lengths of 8,192, 32,768, 131,072 and 1,024,000 bp. For downstream use the paper names three modes: embedding extraction, sequence generation and fine-tuning.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, model architecture, training stages, inference; README_en.md: Model Architecture

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three models are released, each as a Hugging Face checkpoint and a Megatron-LM checkpoint: Genos-1.2B and Genos-10B, trained on human genomes, and Genos-10B-v2 (released 2025-12-18), which adds about 60 billion bases of East Asian genomes, non-human primate genomes and other mammalian genomes, mixed 1:1 with the human corpus. Genos-10B-v2 was trained on 6286B tokens against 2200B for Genos-10B, so results from the two are not interchangeable. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision. The README also announces Gengram (2026-01-30) as a separate model in its own repository.

steps.title: Extract embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

# Specify model path
model_path = "/path/to/your/local/Genos-1.2B" # Replace with local model path

# Load tokenizer and model
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_path)

# Load locally downloaded Genos weights
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(model_path,
                                  output_hidden_states=True,
                                  torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
                                  trust_remote_code=True,
                                  attn_implementation="flash_attention_2" # Use flash_attention
  )
model.cuda() # Load model to GPU
model.eval() # Switch model to inference mode

import random

# Randomly select a specific number of bases
bases = ['A', 'T', 'G', 'C']
seqs = random.choices(bases, k=8192)
# Generate input base sequence
text = ''.join(seqs)

# Encode text
inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt")

# Load data to GPU
inputs = {k: v.cuda() for k, v in inputs.items()}

# Model inference
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs)

# Get hidden states from all layers
hidden_states = outputs.hidden_states  # Tuple containing hidden states from each layer

# Iterate through embeddings from each layer and display key information
for i, layer_embedding in enumerate(hidden_states):
    print(f"Layer {i} embedding ({layer_embedding.shape}): {layer_embedding[0, 0, :10]}")
    print("-" * 50)
PY
steps.explanation: The code cells of the official embedding notebook, steps 1 to 6, joined into one heredoc. Two print lines that only show the input were left out. Replace /path/to/your/local/Genos-1.2B with the folder from the previous step.

outputs: For each layer, the shape of its hidden states ([batch_size, sequence_length, hidden_size]) and the first 10 values for the first position.

profile.summary: ViroHyena is a small family of nucleotide language models built on the Hyena architecture by the authors of the ViroBench viral genomics benchmark. They were pretrained on ViroBlend, a 216 Mbp corpus that mixes human reference, multi-species and viral sequences. The models take nucleotide sequences and serve as baselines in ViroBench for viral taxonomy and host classification from embeddings and for likelihood-based genome modelling.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card introduction; ViroBench README: benchmark description and evaluation protocol

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ViroHyena uses the HyenaDNA model type: stacked Hyena layers over a nucleotide vocabulary of 12 tokens and a maximum of 8192 positions. The four checkpoints differ in width and depth, from d_model 128 with 2 layers to d_model 1024 with 20 layers. The cards tag the models for text generation. In ViroBench, classification is done with the backbone frozen: a sequence embedding is extracted and a small MLP head is trained on it. Generation diagnostics score likelihood in bits per base and test completion of coding sequences.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four checkpoints are on Hugging Face under YDXX: ViroHyena-436k, -1m, -6m and -253m. The model card table lists ViroHyena-436K (0.436M parameters), 1.6M, 6.6M and 253M. profile.summary: RoseTTAFoldNA (also called RF2NA) predicts the three-dimensional structure of proteins, RNA and DNA, alone or bound together in complexes. It takes the sequence of each chain, builds multiple sequence alignments and template searches, and outputs an atomic model in PDB format with per-residue confidence (predicted lDDT) and predicted aligned error. It extends the RoseTTAFold protein structure network to nucleic acids.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; README: Inputs, Expected outputs

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RoseTTAFoldNA uses the three-track design of RoseTTAFold, which refines three representations together: the sequence (1D), pairwise distances between residues (2D) and atom coordinates (3D). The authors extended each track to nucleic acids. The 1D track gains 10 tokens for the four DNA and four RNA nucleotides plus unknown DNA and unknown RNA. The 2D track models base-base and base-amino acid interactions. The 3D track places each nucleotide with a frame on its phosphate group and 10 torsion angles. The network has 36 three-track layers and four refinement layers. It was trained on protein monomers and complexes, RNA monomers and dimers, and protein-RNA and protein-DNA complexes from the PDB, with a generalised all-atom FAPE loss, and inputs include MSAs of related protein and nucleic acid sequences.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, paragraphs on architecture (Fig. 1) and training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists v0.2, dated 13 April 2023, with updated weights (RF2NA_apr23.tgz) for better homodimer-DNA prediction and DNA sequence recognition, MSA pipeline bug fixes and support for paired protein/RNA MSAs. The run script loads network/weights/RF2NA_apr23.pt. The sources do not say which weights the paper's results used. Predictions also depend on the sequence and template databases, which the README downloads at fixed versions for UniRef30 (2020_06) and the PDB templates (pdb100_2021Mar03) but from the current release for Rfam and RNAcentral. A result should name the weights file, the repository commit (this page read f761af28) and the database versions.

strengths.text: One network handles protein-only, RNA-only, protein-RNA and protein-DNA structures, including complexes.

Each prediction comes with confidence estimates (per-residue lDDT and predicted aligned error). The authors report that confident predictions are considerably more accurate than other methods they compared; this is their claim.
Code is MIT licensed and the full pipeline, from MSA generation to the final model, is in the repository.

limitations.text: Setup is heavy: the README downloads UniRef30 (46G), BFD (272G), NCBI nt (151G), RNAcentral (12G) and other databases, and the environment needs CUDA (pytorch-cuda 11.7) and DGL.
The authors say most failures come from poor prediction of single subunits, typically large multidomain proteins, large RNAs (over 100 nt) and small single-stranded nucleic acids.
Training used PDB structures from before May 2020, and the authors point to limited nucleic acid training data.
No licence is stated for the weights file.

run_guide.summary: Install RoseTTAFold2NA and its databases, then predict the structure of the README's example protein-RNA complex.
prerequisites: Linux with conda; the environment file pins python=3.10, pytorch-cuda=11.7 and a CUDA 11.7 build of DGL. GPU type and memory are not stated.
Several hundred gigabytes of disk for the databases: UniRef30 [46G], BFD [272G], nt [151G], RNAcentral [12G], Rfam [300M] and the PDB templates.
The run script uses 8 CPUs and up to 64 GB memory for the MSA tools.

steps.title: Get the code
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/uw-ipd/RoseTTAFold2NA.git
cd RoseTTAFold2NA
git checkout --detach f761af286729ea08a6ddab149023c1b73458fbe2
steps.explanation: Clone and enter the repository as the README says. The checkout line is added to pin the commit this page was written from.

steps.title: Create the environment and install SE(3)-Transformer
steps.shell:
conda env create -f RF2na-linux.yml
conda activate RF2NA
cd SE3Transformer
pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
python setup.py install
cd ..
steps.explanation: Builds the RF2NA conda environment and installs the SE(3)-Transformer copy shipped in the repository.

steps.title: Download the weights
steps.shell:
cd network
wget https://files.ipd.uw.edu/dimaio/RF2NA_apr23.tgz
tar xvfz RF2NA_apr23.tgz
ls weights/ # it should contain a 1.1GB weights file
cd ..
steps.explanation: Downloads and unpacks the v0.2 weights into network/weights.

steps.title: Download the sequence and structure databases
steps.shell:
# uniref30 [46G]
wget http://wwwuser.gwdg.de/~compbiol/uniclust/2020_06/UniRef30_2020_06_hhsuite.tar.gz
mkdir -p UniRef30_2020_06
tar xfz UniRef30_2020_06_hhsuite.tar.gz -C ./UniRef30_2020_06

# BFD [272G]
wget https://bfd.mmseqs.com/bfd_metaclust_clu_complete_id30_c90_final_seq.sorted_opt.tar.gz
mkdir -p bfd
tar xfz bfd_metaclust_clu_complete_id30_c90_final_seq.sorted_opt.tar.gz -C ./bfd

# structure templates (including *_a3m.ffdata, *_a3m.ffindex)
wget https://files.ipd.uw.edu/pub/RoseTTAFold/pdb100_2021Mar03.tar.gz
tar xfz pdb100_2021Mar03.tar.gz

# RNA databases
mkdir -p RNA
cd RNA

# Rfam [300M]
wget ftp://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/Rfam/CURRENT/Rfam.full_region.gz
wget ftp://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/Rfam/CURRENT/Rfam.cm.gz
gunzip Rfam.cm.gz
cmpress Rfam.cm

# RNAcentral [12G]
wget ftp://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/RNAcentral/current_release/rfam/rfam_annotations.tsv.gz
wget ftp://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/RNAcentral/current_release/id_mapping/id_mapping.tsv.gz
wget ftp://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/RNAcentral/current_release/sequences/rnacentral_species_specific_ids.fasta.gz
../input_prep/reprocess_rnac.pl id_mapping.tsv.gz rfam_annotations.tsv.gz   # ~8 minutes
gunzip -c rnacentral_species_specific_ids.fasta.gz | makeblastdb -in - -dbtype nucl  -parse_seqids -out rnacentral.fasta -title "RNACentral"

# nt [151G]
update_blastdb.pl --decompress nt
cd ..
steps.explanation: Downloads and prepares the databases used for MSAs and templates, run from the repository root as in the README. Rfam and RNAcentral come from their current releases, so they change over time.

steps.title: Predict a protein-RNA complex
steps.shell:
conda activate RF2NA
cd example
../run_RF2NA.sh rna_pred rna_binding_protein.fa R:RNA.fa
steps.explanation: Runs the README's protein/RNA example. The first argument is the output folder; the protein FASTA has no tag and the RNA FASTA is tagged R.

profile.summary: 3UTRBERT is an RNA language model for 3' untranslated regions (3'UTRs), the stretch of an mRNA after the coding sequence that carries many regulatory signals. It is a BERT model pre-trained on human 3'UTR sequences, read as overlapping k-mer tokens, and then fine-tuned to predict RNA-binding protein sites, m6A modification sites and where an mRNA sits in the cell. Its attention scores can be used to highlight regions with likely regulatory function.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: 3UTRBERT is the encoder part of a Transformer: token embeddings of dimension 768 plus positional embeddings pass through twelve stacked Transformer layers, each with multi-head self-attention and a feed-forward layer. Sequences are split into overlapping k-mer tokens. It was pre-trained as a masked language model: 15% of the k-mers are masked, in contiguous spans of k tokens so that a masked k-mer cannot be read off its neighbours, and the model learns to restore them; next sentence prediction was dropped. For downstream use, the model is either fine-tuned end to end on short labelled sequences, or frozen and used to extract embeddings for longer sequences.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Experimental Section, Architecture of 3UTRBERT and pre-training; Results 2.1

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four pre-trained checkpoints are linked from the README, for 3-mer, 4-mer, 5-mer and 6-mer tokens. The paper says they share the same architecture and training settings. The 3-mer checkpoint is a single zip file of 322227069 bytes on figshare. Fine-tuning and prediction must use the tokenizer that matches the checkpoint (rna3 to rna6). A result should name the k-mer checkpoint, its figshare version, and the fine-tuning data.

profile.summary: DGRNA is a pretrained RNA language model built for long RNA sequences. It is built mainly from bidirectional Mamba2 layers rather than the Transformer layers of earlier RNA language models, a choice the authors make to handle long sequences efficiently, and was trained on 100 million RNA sequences. Given RNA sequences, the released code returns a per-position representation that can be used for downstream tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: About; bioRxiv abstract; DGRNA/mamba2_pretrained.py: MambaLMHeadModel.forward

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Tokens are embedded and passed through pairs of Mamba2 blocks: one reads the sequence forwards and one reads it reversed. A linear layer merges each pair's outputs. After the last pair, one multi-head attention layer with 32 heads and rotary embeddings is applied, followed by a final normalisation. The model is built on the ESM and Fairseq code bases and uses an ESM-1b style alphabet. The released forward pass returns the hidden states, not token logits. The sources read do not describe the pretraining objective.

name: ERNIE-RNA
description: ERNIE-RNA RNA language model with structure-enhanced representations.

version.note: Family record; the checkpoint is on the configuration

profile.summary: ERNIE-RNA is a pretrained RNA language model that learns from RNA sequence alone but is given a hint about which bases could pair. It is a modified BERT model whose attention is biased by possible base pairs, trained on 20.4 million non-coding RNA sequences. Given RNA sequences up to 1024 nucleotides, it returns sequence and per-base embeddings and attention maps; the repository also ships fine-tuned heads for secondary structure, 3D closeness and 5' UTR mean ribosome load prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Fig. 1, Discussion; README: Embedding Extraction, Secondary structure prediction, 3D Closeness Prediction, UTR MRL prediction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ERNIE-RNA follows the BERT design: 12 transformer blocks, each with 12 attention heads over a 768-dimensional token embedding, about 86 million parameters in total. Its change is an all-against-all pairwise bias added to the attention scores, which gives the model prior knowledge of which bases could pair. It was pretrained with masked language modelling: about 15% of nucleotide tokens are replaced and the model predicts them with a cross-entropy loss. The authors report that the attention maps of the pretrained model already capture secondary structure without fine-tuning.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, The architecture and pre-training of ERNIE-RNA; Methods, pre-training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pretrained checkpoint is released (ERNIE-RNA_pretrain.pt), together with fine-tuned checkpoints: six for secondary structure prediction, each tied to a training set (bpRNA-1m, RNAStralign, RIVAS, RNA3DB, a frozen bpRNA-1m model used for bpRNA-new, and bpRNA-1m plus RNAStralign), one for 3D closeness and one for UTR mean ribosome load. All are downloaded from a Google Drive folder with no version tags. A result should name the checkpoint file, the dataset_name used for structure prediction, and the repository commit; this page read commit 43bc06de.

profile.summary: LAMAR is an RNA language model from the Shanghai Institute of Nutrition and Health (CAS) for studying how RNA processing is regulated. It reads an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and returns an embedding for each nucleotide; fine-tuned versions predict splice sites, translation efficiency from 5' UTRs, mRNA degradation from 3' UTRs and internal ribosome entry sites (IRES). It was pre-trained on about 15 million genome and transcript sequences from 225 mammals and 1569 viruses.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: Model weights; README.md: Compute embeddings; paper: Methods, Model architecture

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LAMAR is a bidirectional Transformer encoder with 12 layers, each with 12 attention heads and a feed-forward size of 3072, and rotary position embeddings. Each nucleotide is one token. During pre-training a portion of nucleotides (15%) is masked and the model predicts them from the surrounding sequence. The code builds the model with an ESM-style model class, EsmModel, from the repository's own LAMAR package. For a downstream task, a task-specific prediction head is placed on the final embeddings and the model is fine-tuned, either with the encoder frozen or with all parameters updated.

sections.body: Two pre-trained models exist: LAMAR-2k (context up to 2048 tokens) and LAMAR-4k (up to 4096 tokens), each saved at training step 250,000. Four fine-tuned models are also published: SpliceSitePred, UTR5TEPred, UTR3DegPred and IRESPred. All six sit in one Hugging Face repository, zhw-e8/LAMAR, as safetensors files under folders named for the run, so a result should give the folder name and the Hugging Face revision. The README's embedding example passes the architecture as arguments that override the base configuration file, which describes a different ESM-2 model (30 layers, hidden size 640); a user must keep those overrides.

steps.title: Compute embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from LAMAR.modeling_nucESM2 import EsmModel
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoTokenizer
from safetensors.torch import load_file, load_model
import torch


seq = "ATACGATGCTAGCTAGTGACTAGCTGATCGTAGCTG"
model_max_length = 1026
device = torch.device("cuda:0")
# instance tokenizer and config
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("tokenizer/single_nucleotide/", model_max_length=model_max_length)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(
    "config/config_150M.json", vocab_size=len(tokenizer), pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id,
    mask_token_id=tokenizer.mask_token_id, token_dropout=False, positional_embedding_type='rotary',
    hidden_size=768, intermediate_size=3072, num_attention_heads=12, num_hidden_layers=12
)
# intance the model and load pretrained weights
model = EsmModel(config)
weights = load_file('pretrain/saving_model/mammalian80D_4096len1mer1sw_80M/checkpoint-250000/model.safetensors')
weights_dict = {}
for k, v in weights.items():
    new_k = k.replace('esm.', '') if 'esm' in k else k
    weights_dict[new_k] = v
model.load_state_dict(weights_dict, strict=False)
model = model.to(device)
# Compute embeddings
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    inputs = tokenizer(seq, return_tensors="pt")
    input_ids = inputs['input_ids'].to(device)
    attention_mask = inputs['attention_mask'].to(device)
    outputs = model(
        input_ids=input_ids,
        attention_mask=attention_mask
    )
    embedding = outputs.last_hidden_state[0, 1 : -1, :]
print(embedding.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's embedding example, run from the repository root in a heredoc, with a final print of the embedding shape added.

outputs: A tensor of per-nucleotide embeddings for the input sequence, without the special start and end tokens; the added print shows its shape.

profile.summary: PlantRNA-FM is an RNA language model for plants. It was pretrained on transcript sequences from 1,124 plant species, together with predicted secondary structure and labels for the 5' UTR, coding sequence and 3' UTR. It reads an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and outputs per-nucleotide embeddings, which the authors fine-tune for tasks such as genic region annotation and translation efficiency, and use to find RNA sequence and structure motifs linked to translation.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results 'PlantRNA-FM integrates 1,124 plant transcriptomes'; Methods 'RNA tokenization'; Discussion; README: Inference

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PlantRNA-FM is an encoder-only transformer with 12 layers and an embedding dimension of 480. Each nucleotide is one token, and positions are encoded with rotary position embedding. Pretraining used three objectives together: masked nucleotide modelling, in which 20% of nucleotides in each sequence are selected for masking and reconstructed; prediction of the RNA secondary structure, which the authors annotated with ViennaRNA (RNAfold); and classification of each nucleotide into CDS, 5' UTR or 3' UTR. For a downstream task the authors replace the output layer and fine-tune the model. To find motifs, they use the model's attention contrast matrix with unsupervised hierarchical clustering.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Model architecture', 'RNA tokenization', 'Pretraining strategies of PlantRNA-FM', 'Fine tuning of downstream tasks'; README: Model Overview

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is published, yangheng/PlantRNA-FM on Hugging Face; this page read it at revision 5e7baf4e. The model card points users to a newer model from the same group, OmniGenome-186M, also trained on OneKP; it is a separate model and not described here. The sources disagree on some details. The paper and model card describe 24 attention heads, while the published config.json sets 20. The GitHub README says the model handles up to 512 nucleotides, while the paper says pretraining used 512 and fine-tuning allowed up to 1,026 tokens, the model card says up to 1026 nucleotides, and config.json sets max_position_embeddings to 1026. A result should name the Hugging Face revision. The GitHub repository holds the fine-tuning datasets and task scripts; the paper says training and inference code is in the Hugging Face repository.

profile.summary: ProtRNA is an RNA language model made by adapting a protein language model, ESM-2, to RNA sequences. The authors' idea is that information learned from the much larger body of protein sequences can transfer to RNA, where sequences are fewer and less conserved. It takes RNA sequences and returns per-nucleotide embeddings, which the repository uses for secondary structure, protein-RNA interaction and mean ribosome loading prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Abstract, Inference, Evaluation; bioRxiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProtRNA starts from the ESM-2 protein language model and is trained further on RNA by a cross-modality transfer learning strategy. In the released code the model keeps the ESM-2 vocabulary of amino acids and appends lower-case RNA tokens (a, u, g, c, x), so the same alphabet holds both kinds of sequence. Input RNA is lower-cased, T is mapped to u, and any other character becomes x. The pretrained model built by the loader has 33 layers, embedding dimension 1280 and 20 attention heads. Embeddings from layer 33 feed separate prediction heads for each downstream task. The sources read do not describe the RNA training objective or data in detail.
sections.source_locator: README: Abstract, Inference; pretrained.py load_pretrained_model; protrna/data.py Alphabet.from_architecture and _to_rna_vocab

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pretrained language model is released, ProtRNA_pretrained.h5, as TensorFlow weights on Zenodo record 14795554. The same record holds task heads: four RotaFormer secondary structure heads trained on different datasets and selected under different metrics, protein-RNA interaction heads for 17 RBPs in HeLa cells, and a mean ribosome loading head (the last two in PyTorch). The README notes that an earlier version of the paper scored secondary structure with the authors' own metrics and keeps a script for that. A result should name the Zenodo record, the head file and the repository commit; this page read commit 991037d6. The preprint has two bioRxiv versions, and the bioRxiv record links a published version, DOI 10.1016/j.cels.2025.101371.

profile.summary: RFamLlama is a generative RNA language model conditioned on RNA family. Given an Rfam family ID as a prompt tag, it writes new RNA sequences of that family; the same model can also score sequences for zero-shot fitness prediction. It was trained on sequences from over 4,000 RNA families, each labelled with a family tag.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card introduction; workshop abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RFamLlama is a decoder-only Llama model for causal (next-token) language modelling over a 22-token vocabulary. Each training sequence is preceded by a control tag naming its family. A prompt has the form <|bos|> <|tag_start|> family number <|tag_end|> <|5|>, where the family number is the Rfam ID without the RF prefix; the model then writes the sequence, which ends at the <|3|> token. The developers report that the family tags improve zero-shot fitness prediction; the sources read do not say how a fitness score is computed.

Both use the same tokenizer and prompt format. Generation is sampled (do_sample=True), so a result should name the checkpoint, its revision and the sampling settings.

run_guide.summary: Load RFamLlama-base from Hugging Face and sample ten tRNA-family (RF00005) sequences.
prerequisites: Python with PyTorch and transformers; the sources give no versions or install command. The checkpoints were saved with transformers 4.38.2.
A CUDA GPU is used when available; otherwise the example runs on CPU.
Non-commercial use only, under CC-BY-NC-4.0.

steps.title: Generate sequences for one Rfam family
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
# generation
from transformers import LlamaForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, pipeline
import torch
import sys

model_url = "jinyuan22/RFamLlama-base"
model = LlamaForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_url, torch_dtype=torch.float16)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_url)

device = torch.device("cuda:0") if torch.cuda.is_available() else torch.device("cpu")

pipe = pipeline("text-generation", model=model, device=device, tokenizer=tokenizer)

tag = "RF00005"
txt = f"<|bos|> <|tag_start|> {tag[2:]} <|tag_end|> <|5|> "
all_outputs = []
outputs = pipe(txt, num_return_sequences=10, max_new_tokens=300, repetition_penalty=1, top_p=1,temperature=1, do_sample=True)

for i, output in enumerate(outputs):
    seq = output["generated_text"]
    seq = seq.split("<|5|>")[1].split("<|3|>")[0]
    print(f">{i}\n{seq}")
PY
steps.explanation: The model card's example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. Replace RF00005 with another Rfam ID, or the model URL with jinyuan22/RFamLlama-large, to change family or size. It downloads the latest revision.

outputs: Ten sampled sequences printed in FASTA style, with headers >0 to >9.

Outputs are random samples and change between runs unless a seed is set; the card sets none.

profile.summary: Uni-RNA is a pre-trained language model for RNA sequences from DP Technology. It reads an RNA sequence and returns a learned representation (embedding) for each position, or predicted probabilities for masked positions. The authors fine-tune these representations for RNA structure and function prediction tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: bioRxiv abstract; README.md: Model summary and Quick Start

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Uni-RNA is a Transformer encoder with a masked-language-model head: the masked-LM class outputs, for each position, logits over the token vocabulary. The released configurations use 64-dimensional attention heads, a GELU feed-forward layer three times the hidden size, rotary position embeddings and a vocabulary of 10 tokens; in the L16 upload these are five special tokens and the letters N, A, T, C, G and U. The last hidden layer gives per-position embeddings that can be used directly or fine-tuned for a downstream task. The training data and pre-training details are described in the preprint, whose full text was not read here.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Model summary, Quick Start; bioRxiv abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three checkpoints are released: L8 (8 layers, hidden size 512), L12 (12 layers, hidden size 768) and L16 (16 layers, hidden size 1024). The repository distributes them together as one weights archive on Google Drive, with no version label. Uploads named UniRNA-L8, UniRNA-L12 and UniRNA-L16 also exist on Hugging Face under the EscheWang account, but the repository README does not link to them. A result should name the checkpoint (L8, L12 or L16) and where the weights came from.

name: DeepVariant
description: Deep-learning variant caller that classifies pileup images with a convolutional network.

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: DeepVariant is a germline variant caller: it finds SNPs and small indels in a person's sequencing reads. It takes reads aligned to a reference genome, turns the reads around each candidate site into a pileup image, classifies that image with a convolutional neural network, and writes the calls to a VCF or gVCF file. Trained models are provided for short-read, long-read and other sequencing technologies, all trained on human data.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and notes; paper title

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DeepVariant runs as three programs. make_examples reads the aligned reads and the reference and writes a multi-channel tensor for each candidate site. All models use six base channels (read base, base quality, mapping quality, strand, whether the read supports the allele, and whether the base matches the reference); Illumina models add an insert size channel and PacBio and ONT models add a haplotype channel. call_variants classifies each tensor with a convolutional network and is the only step that uses a GPU. The usage guide's section on changes since the 2016 precisionFDA challenge says the model moved to the Inception-v3 architecture; the sources read do not state the architecture of the v1.10 models. postprocess_variants sorts the results, combines multi-allelic records and writes a VCF, and optionally a gVCF. Genotypes are limited to hom-ref, het and hom-alt.
sections.source_locator: deepvariant-details.md: Inputs and outputs, Updates since the precisionFDA challenge; quick start: Notes on GPU image; README.md: notes

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: DeepVariant is released as numbered versions; the README read is for v1.10, with Docker image google/deepvariant:1.10.0. Each release bundles its models inside the Docker image, selected with --model_type: WGS, WES, PACBIO, ONT_R104 or HYBRID_PACBIO_ILLUMINA. Model files for all releases are also kept in a public Google Cloud bucket. Training data change between releases, so a result must name the release version and the model type.

run_guide.summary: Pull the DeepVariant 1.10.0 Docker image, download the small test bundle and call variants in a 10 kb region of chromosome 20.
prerequisites: A Unix-like machine with the AVX instruction set and Docker (the quick start installs docker.io with apt).
No GPU needed; a GPU image exists for the call_variants step.
Network access to Docker Hub and storage.googleapis.com.
Code is BSD-3-Clause; no separate licence for the models is stated.

steps.title: Get the Docker image
steps.shell:
BIN_VERSION="1.10.0"

sudo apt -y update
sudo apt-get -y install docker.io
sudo docker pull google/deepvariant:"${BIN_VERSION}"
steps.explanation: Copied from the quick start. The models are inside the image.

steps.title: Download the test bundle
steps.shell:
INPUT_DIR="${PWD}/quickstart-testdata"
DATA_HTTP_DIR="https://storage.googleapis.com/deepvariant/quickstart-testdata"

mkdir -p ${INPUT_DIR}
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/NA12878_S1.chr20.10_10p1mb.bam
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/NA12878_S1.chr20.10_10p1mb.bam.bai
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/ucsc.hg19.chr20.unittest.fasta
wget -P ${INPUT_DIR} "${DATA_HTTP_DIR}"/ucsc.hg19.chr20.unittest.fasta.fai
steps.explanation: A subset of the quick start's download lines: the BAM, its index, the reference FASTA and its index, which the run step uses. The quick start also downloads truth files for evaluation with hap.py.

steps.title: Call variants
steps.shell:
OUTPUT_DIR="${PWD}/quickstart-output"
mkdir -p "${OUTPUT_DIR}"

sudo docker run \
  -v "${INPUT_DIR}":"/input" \
  -v "${OUTPUT_DIR}":"/output" \
  google/deepvariant:"${BIN_VERSION}" \
  /opt/deepvariant/bin/run_deepvariant \
  --model_type=WGS \
  --vcf_stats_report=true \
  --ref=/input/ucsc.hg19.chr20.unittest.fasta \
  --reads=/input/NA12878_S1.chr20.10_10p1mb.bam \
  --regions "chr20:10,000,000-10,010,000" \
  --output_vcf=/output/output.vcf.gz \
  --output_gvcf=/output/output.g.vcf.gz \
  --intermediate_results_dir /output/intermediate_results_dir \
  --num_shards=1
steps.explanation: Copied from the quick start. run_deepvariant runs make_examples, call_variants and postprocess_variants in turn.
steps.source_locator: deepvariant-quick-start.md: Run DeepVariant with one command

name: ModernGENA
description: BERT-style DNA language model built on the ModernBERT backbone with a 32k BPE vocabulary.

attributes.access: Checkpoints for ModernGENA base and large on Hugging Face (DNA language models collection)

version.note: Family record; sizes are on configurations

profile.summary: ModernGENA is a DNA language model that adapts the ModernBERT encoder to genomic sequences. It reads DNA split into byte-pair-encoding (BPE) tokens and was pretrained by masked language modelling on 443 vertebrate genome assemblies. It outputs token embeddings that are fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as sequence classification or per-token regression; the authors present it as an efficient baseline for future DNA model work.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC abstract; model card: Tokenization, Pretraining corpus; GENA_LM examples README

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ModernGENA is a BERT-style encoder built on ModernBERT. The model card lists RoPE positional embeddings, hybrid local and global attention, pre-norm transformer blocks, GeGLU feed-forward layers and end-to-end unpadding, with FlashAttention for faster inference on compatible hardware. In the published configurations, local attention covers 128 tokens and every third layer uses global attention. Input DNA is tokenised with the 32k BPE vocabulary from GENA-LM over the symbols A, T, G, C and N. Pretraining used masked language modelling on intervals sampled from -16 kbp to +8 kbp around each transcription start site, on both strands, to reduce the weight of simple repeats.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Technical features, Tokenization, Pretraining corpus; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two checkpoints are released on Hugging Face: ModernGENA base (22 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads) and ModernGENA large (28 layers, hidden size 1024, 16 attention heads). Both use the same tokenizer, the same pretraining corpus description and a vocabulary of 32768 tokens. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision; this page read base at revision 7036ebb6 and large at revision 01de8202. The paper says the full implementation and configuration are released; the fine-tuning examples the card links to live in the GENA_LM repository.

Two negative controls confirmed it fails on a swapped pair of values and on a cell shifted into the neighbouring column. profile.summary: Borzoi is a neural network that predicts RNA-seq coverage, the read depth along genes in different cell types and tissues, directly from DNA sequence. It takes a 524 kb stretch of human or mouse genome and outputs predicted coverage for thousands of experiments in 32 bp bins. Comparing predictions for the reference and the variant sequence gives scores for a variant's effect on gene expression, splicing and polyadenylation.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; README.md: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Borzoi is a supervised model, not a language model: it is trained to reproduce measured coverage tracks. It uses the core Enformer architecture, a tower of convolution and pooling blocks followed by self-attention blocks at 128 bp resolution, then a U-net that upsamples back to 32 bp resolution. The training targets are RNA-seq coverage from ENCODE and GTEx plus the Enformer training data (CAGE, DNase-seq, ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq). Variant effects are computed from the difference between predicted coverage for the reference and the alternate sequence, summarised by statistics such as logSED for gene expression, COVR for polyadenylation and nDi for splicing.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Main, model description; README.md: introduction; legacy score_variants tutorial

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The published model is four replicates trained with identical data splits, each distributed as a human and a mouse .h5 weight file. The authors report that an ensemble of the four replicates generally performed better than any single replicate. A separate collection of smaller Mini Borzoi models, trained on subsets of data types or with architecture changes, is also published. The repository has legacy and latest data transforms; the legacy transforms match the manuscript. A result should say which replicates were used, whether they were averaged, and which transform was applied.

name: Caduceus
description: Self-supervised DNA language model pretrained on human genomic sequence.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: Caduceus is a family of DNA language models for long human genomic sequences. It reads DNA one base at a time, looking both upstream and downstream, and is built so that a sequence and its reverse complement are treated consistently. The pretrained models output masked-base predictions and per-base embeddings that can be fine-tuned or used as features, for example for variant effect prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; model card: Model Details; README: eQTL SNP Variant Effect Prediction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Caduceus builds on the long-range Mamba block. The authors extend it to a BiMamba component that reads a sequence in both directions, and to a MambaDNA block that is also reverse-complement (RC) equivariant. The published checkpoints have hidden dimension 256 and 16 MambaDNA layers and were pretrained as masked language models on the human reference genome. In the RC-equivariant Caduceus-PS model the hidden state is twice the width of a non-equivariant model, and the card says to run a downstream model on the hidden state and its reverse complement, or average them, to get RC-invariant outputs.
sections.source_locator: arXiv abstract; model card: Model Details; README: Using Caduceus with Hugging Face

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists two pretrained checkpoints on Hugging Face. Caduceus-Ph was trained with reverse-complement data augmentation. Caduceus-PS is RC equivariant by design and needs no augmentation. Both were trained on sequences of length 131k with model size 256 and 16 layers, for 50k steps at batch size 8. A result should name the checkpoint (Ph or PS) and its Hugging Face revision; this page read PS at revision d89eeb85 and Ph at revision b0477522. The repository also holds the training code used to reproduce the paper's pretraining and fine-tuning experiments.

name: Enformer
description: Convolution and Transformer model trained to predict genomic tracks from sequences of up to about 200 kb.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3; Tang et al. Table 1 and Methods

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: Enformer is a neural network that predicts gene expression and other genomic signals directly from DNA sequence. It reads about 200 kb of sequence and predicts 5,313 human (or 1,643 mouse) tracks, such as CAGE, DNase-seq, ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq signal, in 128 bp bins across the central 114,688 bp. Comparing predictions for reference and alternate sequences gives variant effect scores, and precomputed scores are published for common 1000 Genomes variants.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Methods, Model architecture; README.md: Pre-computed variant effect predictions

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Enformer is a supervised model trained to reproduce measured genomic tracks. It has three parts: seven convolutional blocks with pooling that reduce 196,608 bp to 1,536 positions of 128 bp each, eleven transformer blocks that let distant positions exchange information, and a cropping layer followed by pointwise convolutions into separate human and mouse output heads. The transformer layers use relative positional basis functions and give a receptive field that reaches elements up to 100 kb away. It was trained jointly on human and mouse data from the Basenji2 dataset, with the input extended to 196,608 bp.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model architecture and Training; Results

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pre-trained model is published, at https://tfhub.dev/deepmind/enformer/1, with code to load its weights into the Sonnet Enformer module for fine-tuning. The README's inference example passes 393,216 bp, of which the model uses only the central 196,608 bp. Precomputed SAD and SAR variant scores on hg19 and their top 20 principal components are published for frequent 1000 Genomes variants. The paper also describes fine-tuning the model on human data. A result should state the model URL and version, whether published scores were used, and the genome build.

name: GENA-LM
description: Transformer DNA language models in BERT-base, BERT-large and BigBird variants.

attributes.source_locator: Manzo et al. Table 2 and Table 3

version.note: Family record; versions are on configurations

profile.summary: GENA-LM is a family of transformer DNA language models for reading long genomic sequences, up to 36,000 base pairs in its sparse-attention versions. It takes DNA split into variable-length tokens and returns sequence representations that are fine-tuned for tasks such as promoter, splice site, enhancer and chromatin profile prediction. Most models were trained on the human T2T genome, and species-specific and multispecies models also exist.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Materials and methods (Sequence tokenization); README_previous_generation.md: Pre-trained models, Downstream tasks

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GENA-LM models are BERT-style transformer encoders trained as masked language models. DNA is first split by a Byte-Pair Encoding tokenizer with a dictionary of 32 000 tokens, so one token covers several bases; the paper reports a median token length of 9 bp. BERT models use pre-layer normalisation. Three models reach 4096 tokens (about 36,000 bp): two use DeepSpeed sparse attention with rotary position embeddings, and bigbird-base-t2t uses the Hugging Face BigBird implementation. The paper also describes fine-tuning with a recurrent memory mechanism to process even longer segments.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sequence tokenization, Abstract; README_previous_generation.md: Pre-trained models

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository table lists eight pretrained checkpoints: five BERT models of 512 tokens (4500 bp) and three BigBird-style models of 4096 tokens (36000 bp). They differ in depth (12 or 24 layers), in the data used for the tokenizer and for training (T2T only, T2T with 1000 Genomes SNPs, or with multispecies data), and in which chromosomes were held out. The paper also names yeast, fly and Arabidopsis models. Fine-tuned checkpoints for promoters and splice sites are kept as branches of the Hugging Face repositories. A result should name the checkpoint, the branch if any, and the Hugging Face revision; this page read gena-lm-bert-base-t2t at revision 4f1352bd. The developers have since released a successor family, modernGENA, in the same repository.

strengths.text: BPE tokens cover about 9 bp on median, so the BERT models see about 4500 bp in 512 tokens, and the BigBird models about 36000 bp.
Several training-data choices are released side by side, including human-only, multispecies and taxon-specific models for yeast, Arabidopsis and Drosophila.
The BERT and bigbird-base-t2t checkpoints load with the transformers library, and fine-tuned promoter and splice site checkpoints are published as branches.
strengths.source_locator: README_previous_generation.md: Examples, Pre-trained models on downstream tasks

limitations.text: The sparse-attention models need DeepSpeed, FP16 and a GPU of compute capability 7 or above, with old PyTorch and CUDA versions.
BPE tokens vary in length from 1 bp to 64 bp, so one model output position does not correspond to a fixed number of bases.
The developers now present GENA-LM as their previous generation and lead the repository with modernGENA.
No weights licence is declared on the model card read, so terms of reuse for the weights are unclear.
